            {"role": "user", "content": document},
        ],
        Invoice,
    )


async def main() -> None:
    """Extract with Claude."""
    print(await read(AnthropicGenerator(api_key="sk-ant-..."), "Invoice A-1, $5.00"))


asyncio.run(main())

Each provider asks for JSON differently, and the backend handles it:

  • Anthropic — output_config.format with type: json_schema. The API requires additionalProperties: false on every object and rejects numeric and string-length constraints (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs); the schema sent is adapted, and the reply is validated against your model, original constraints included.
  • OpenAI — response_format with type: json_schema.
  • DeepSeek — response_format with type: json_object, the only JSON mode documented (https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/json_mode); the schema goes in a system turn at the end of the conversation, which also meets the requirement of the word "json" in the prompt.

docs.title: Full outcome, images and the provider from the model id
docs.text:
chat_structured answers one question — "give me the instance" — and raises on any other outcome. Whoever pays for each call needs three more answers, even when there is no instance: what the call cost, why the model stopped and what it wrote. A refusal, a reply cut at max_tokens or JSON that fails the schema were billed too.

complete_structured returns all of it in a StructuredCompletion, and hosted_generator picks the provider from the model id:

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path

from pydantic import BaseModel

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import BaseAppSettings, HostedGenAISettings
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import (
    StructuredCompletion,
    StructuredCompletionBackend,
    hosted_generator,
    image_part,
)


class Settings(HostedGenAISettings, BaseAppSettings):
    """Service settings."""

    AI_MODEL: str = "claude-haiku-5-5"


class Transcript(BaseModel):
    """The text read from the photo."""

    readable: bool
    text: str


async def transcribe(
    backend: StructuredCompletionBackend,
    photo: bytes,
) -> StructuredCompletion[Transcript]:
    """Read the text of a notebook photo."""
    return await backend.complete_structured(
        [
            {"role": "system", "content": "Transcribe the text in the photo."},
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": [
                    image_part(photo, "image/jpeg"),
                    {"type": "text", "text": "Transcribe it."},
                ],
            },
        ],
        Transcript,
        effort="low",
        cache_system=True,
        max_tokens=2048,
    )


async def main() -> None:
    """Transcribe with the configured model."""
    settings = Settings()
    backend = hosted_generator(**settings.hosted_kwargs(settings.AI_MODEL))
    result = await transcribe(backend, Path("notebook.jpg").read_bytes())
    if result.output is not None:
        print(result.output.text)
    else:
        print("no result:", result.stop_reason, result.error)
    print("tokens:", result.usage)


asyncio.run(main())

Piece by piece:

  • hosted_generator(model, api_key=...) reads the provider off the id prefix (claude- → Anthropic, gpt-/o1/o3/o4/chatgpt- → OpenAI, gemini- → Google, deepseek- → DeepSeek; the table is MODEL_PREFIXES) and builds the backend with what each provider documents: the field the output budget goes to (max_completion_tokens on OpenAI), the JSON mode (json_object on DeepSeek) and the effort values. An id outside the table (a fine-tune, your own server) raises ValueError: pass provider= and, if needed, base_url=.
  • settings.hosted_kwargs(model) returns exactly the arguments of hosted_generator — the model, and the key and URL of the resolved provider. Changing provider becomes changing AI_MODEL in .env (and having that provider's key there).
  • image_part(data, media_type) builds the image part in the OpenAI shape, which is the SDK's message shape. AnthropicGenerator translates it to a Messages API image block; OpenAICompatGenerator forwards it as is.
  • effort goes out as output_config.effort on Anthropic and as reasoning_effort on the OpenAI format. Gemini documents minimal, low, medium and high (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/openai), so xhigh and max become high (GOOGLE_EFFORT_VALUES). DeepSeek does not document the field, and neither hosted_generator nor deepseek_kwargs() sends it (effort_field=None).
  • cache_system=True marks the system turn with cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"} on Anthropic. The OpenAI format has no per-message marker, and the argument is accepted and ignored.

The StructuredCompletion you get back:

Field What it is output the validated instance, or None text the reply as received usage the provider's TokenUsage, whatever the outcome; None when the response carries no usage stop_reason end, max_tokens, refusal, tool_use or other provider_stop_reason the original value (end_turn, length...) error why output is None after a natural stop

Only a natural stop is parsed

A reply cut at max_tokens can validate by accident when the schema's last fields have defaults. So parsing only happens with stop_reason == "end"; otherwise output is None and error stays empty — stop_reason already says why.

Cache written and cache read

TokenUsage.cache_write_tokens is the slice of the input written to the cache (Anthropic's cache_creation_input_tokens), which Anthropic bills above the base rate; cache_hit_tokens is the slice read. Both are already inside input_tokens. The OpenAI format reports no write, and the field stays 0.

The tests for this surface run over httpx.MockTransport: they pin the request each backend builds and the reading of the documented response, not the behavior of a live provider.

docs.title: One provider chosen in .env
docs.text:
Reading the provider off the model id prefix is convenient, but it hides a business decision inside a model name, and each provider wants its own key variable. When the service sends every model to one provider, say so in .env, with the provider, the key and (optionally) the URL:

# .env
GENAI_PROVIDER=openai
GENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
# GENAI_BASE_URL=https://internal-gateway/v1   # empty uses the provider URL
AI_MODEL_FREE=gpt-5-mini
AI_MODEL_FAMILY=gpt-5

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import BaseAppSettings, HostedGenAISettings
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import TextBackend, hosted_generator


class Settings(HostedGenAISettings, BaseAppSettings):
    """Service settings: both models come from the same provider."""

    AI_MODEL_FREE: str = "gpt-5-mini"
    AI_MODEL_FAMILY: str = "gpt-5"


def plan_backend(settings: Settings, family: bool) -> TextBackend:
    """Build the plan's generator with the provider from `.env`."""
    model = settings.AI_MODEL_FAMILY if family else settings.AI_MODEL_FREE
    return hosted_generator(**settings.hosted_kwargs(model))


settings = Settings(GENAI_PROVIDER="openai", GENAI_API_KEY="sk-...")
print(settings.hosted_kwargs(settings.AI_MODEL_FREE)["provider"])  # openai

With GENAI_PROVIDER set, hosted_kwargs changes rule:

  • The provider is the one in .env, for every model. An id with another provider's prefix (claude-... with GENAI_PROVIDER=openai) raises ValueError instead of switching provider silently; an id with no known prefix (a fine-tune, a model behind an OpenAI-compatible server) goes to the chosen provider.
  • The key is GENAI_API_KEY; empty, it falls back to the provider's own key (OPENAI_API_KEY...). The URL is GENAI_BASE_URL or, when empty, the provider's.
  • A provider= that disagrees with .env raises ValueError: one service talks to one provider.
  • Without GENAI_PROVIDER (absent or empty), nothing changes: the provider comes from the prefix, as in the section above.

The production boot demands the key

With EnvironmentSettings composed and ENV=production, a GENAI_PROVIDER with no effective key (neither GENAI_API_KEY nor the provider's own) refuses the boot, listing GENAI_API_KEY. A service that never sets GENAI_PROVIDER is not affected: the per-provider keys stay optional.

docs.title: PDFs: document_part and supports_documents
docs.text:
You already send images with image_part. PDFs have the same problem, plus one: each provider spells the document part its own way, and not every provider takes one. Writing the block by hand (Anthropic's document, for instance) ties the service to one provider — changing GENAI_PROVIDER then breaks only the PDF flow, and only in production.

document_part builds the part once, and each generator translates it or refuses it:

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path

from pydantic import BaseModel

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import BaseAppSettings, HostedGenAISettings
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import (
    StructuredCompletion,
    StructuredCompletionBackend,
    document_part,
    hosted_generator,
    supports_documents,
)


class Settings(HostedGenAISettings, BaseAppSettings):
    """The service settings."""

    AI_MODEL: str = "claude-haiku-5-5"


class Agenda(BaseModel):
    """The events read from the notice."""

    events: list[str]


async def read_agenda(
    backend: StructuredCompletionBackend,
    pdf: bytes,
) -> StructuredCompletion[Agenda]:
    """Extract the events from a PDF notice."""
    return await backend.complete_structured(
        [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": [
                    document_part(pdf, filename="notice.pdf"),
                    {"type": "text", "text": "List the events."},
                ],
            },
        ],
        Agenda,
        max_tokens=2048,
    )


async def main() -> None:
    """Check the provider at boot and read the PDF."""
    settings = Settings()
    kwargs = settings.hosted_kwargs(settings.AI_MODEL)
    if not supports_documents(kwargs["provider"]):
        raise SystemExit(f"{kwargs['provider']} documents no PDF input")
    backend = hosted_generator(**kwargs)
    result = await read_agenda(backend, Path("notice.pdf").read_bytes())
    print(result.output)


asyncio.run(main())

Piece by piece:

  • document_part(data, media_type="application/pdf", *, filename=None) builds OpenAI's Chat Completions file part: file_data is a base64 data URL and filename goes with it (document.pdf when you pass none, because every base64 example in OpenAI's guide sends a name). Only application/pdf is accepted; another type, or empty bytes, raises ValueError right away. Plain text goes in a text part.
  • Anthropic: AnthropicGenerator translates the part into a document block with a base64 source, and filename becomes the block's title.
  • OpenAI: OpenAICompatGenerator forwards the part as is.
  • Google and DeepSeek: the generator hosted_generator builds for them (and the one google_kwargs() / deepseek_kwargs() build) raises ValueError before opening the connection when a message carries the part, with a message naming the provider. Text and images still go out normally.
  • supports_documents(provider) answers the same question without calling anything: True for anthropic and openai, False for google, deepseek, None and an unknown name. It is what the service checks at boot, or before offering the PDF route. The list is DOCUMENT_PROVIDERS.

Where each row came from, read on 2026-11-04:

Provider What the documentation says SDK result Anthropic document block with a base64 application/pdf source, according to Anthropic's documentation (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support) translates OpenAI "Chat Completions accepts only PDF files as file content parts", with file_data as a data URL, according to OpenAI's documentation (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/pdf-files) forwards Google the compatible-endpoint page (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/openai) documents image and audio, and no file part ValueError DeepSeek the chat reference (https://api-docs.deepseek.com/api/create-chat-completion) lists a file part, but describes file_data as a data URL "of the image" and names no PDF ValueError

The request was tested, not the answer

The tests for this part run on httpx.MockTransport: they pin the body each generator builds and the ValueError with no request sent. No provider was actually called — that Anthropic and OpenAI read the PDF is what their documentation says, not something the SDK measured. If Google or DeepSeek start documenting PDFs, the change is one line in DOCUMENT_PROVIDERS.

Generic compatible server

An OpenAICompatGenerator built by hand (vLLM, your own gateway) forwards the part by default (accepts_documents=True): the SDK does not know what that server accepts, and the server answers for it. Pass accepts_documents=False to refuse before the call.

docs.title: Embeddings (OpenAI)
docs.text:
OpenAICompatEmbedder implements SupportsEmbed, so it goes into a Retriever in place of OllamaEmbedder:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OpenAICompatEmbedder


async def main() -> None:
    """Produce two vectors."""
    embedder: OpenAICompatEmbedder = OpenAICompatEmbedder(
        "text-embedding-3-small",
        api_key="sk-...",
    )
    vectors: list[list[float]] = await embedder.embed(["hello", "world"])
    print(len(vectors))


asyncio.run(main())

Vectors come back in input order, sorted by the response's index.

Anthropic and DeepSeek have no embeddings

Anthropic offers no embedding endpoint, and the navigation of DeepSeek's reference lists Chat Completions, Responses, FIM, models, balance and files — no embeddings. For RAG with those providers, produce the vectors with OpenAICompatEmbedder, OllamaEmbedder or Embedder.

docs.title: When the provider fails
docs.text:
Both backends raise the same exception family:

Exception Status What to do HostedAuthenticationError 401, 403 Fix the key — retrying will not help HostedRateLimitError 429 Wait retry_after seconds (when the header is sent) HostedServerError 5xx, including Anthropic's 529 Try later, or fall back to another backend HostedAPIError anything else (400, 402, 422...) Fix the request

All inherit from HostedAPIError, which inherits from httpx.HTTPStatusError — code that already caught that exception from OpenAICompatGenerator keeps catching it.

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import (
    AnthropicGenerator,
    HostedRateLimitError,
    HostedServerError,
    OllamaGenerator,
)


async def answer(question: str) -> str:
    """Use Claude and fall back to local Ollama when it is down."""
    claude: AnthropicGenerator = AnthropicGenerator(api_key="sk-ant-...")
    try:
        return await claude.generate(question)
    except HostedRateLimitError as error:
        print(f"rate limited; retry in {error.retry_after}s")
        raise
    except HostedServerError:
        return await OllamaGenerator("llama3.2").generate(question)


print(asyncio.run(answer("Explain PIX.")))

Each exception carries provider, status_code, error_type and detail (from the provider's error body) and request_id (Anthropic's request-id header). On Anthropic, an error can also arrive after the 200, in the middle of the stream (event: error, https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming): stream() raises the same typed exception — an overloaded_error becomes a HostedServerError with status_code 529 — and the text already yielded stays yielded.

Retry is built in

The SDK's HTTP client retries 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504 with exponential backoff — on AnthropicGenerator, 529 too. What it does not retry is a read timeout: the provider aborts the generation when the client gives up, and the retry would start it again from zero.

docs.title: Why not the official SDKs
docs.text: anthropic and openai are HTTP wrappers. At their current versions (anthropic 1.15.0, openai 3.31.0), both require httpx2 — a second HTTP stack that the SDK's HTTPClient and the tests' httpx.MockTransport do not reach — plus jiter, anyio and sniffio with upper bounds. What the SDK uses from them is one POST and an SSE reader. Building on the httpx that is already a dependency keeps retry, circuit-breaker and X-Request-ID the same as Ollama's, and puts no upper bound in any consumer's lock.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• AnthropicGenerator and OpenAICompatGenerator implement the same protocols as OllamaGenerator: change the construction, keep the rest.
  • HostedGenAISettings + anthropic_kwargs() / openai_kwargs() / deepseek_kwargs() / google_kwargs() build the backend by splat.
  • GENAI_PROVIDER + GENAI_API_KEY (+ GENAI_BASE_URL) pin one provider for every model from .env; another provider's model raises.
  • hosted_generator(**settings.hosted_kwargs(model)) picks the provider from the model id; complete_structured returns output, usage and stop reason whatever the outcome (usage, when the provider reports it), with images through image_part.
  • PDFs go through document_part: a document block on Anthropic, a file part on OpenAI, ValueError before the call on Google and DeepSeek; supports_documents(provider) answers at boot.
  • Tool calling, structured output and streaming work on all four (on Gemini, tool calling and streaming go through the compatible endpoint without a test of their own); embeddings only on OpenAI (OpenAICompatEmbedder).
  • Failures become HostedAuthenticationError, HostedRateLimitError or HostedServerError — mid-stream included.

docs.title: Self-hosted generative AI
docs.text:
Run HuggingFace models on your own hardware — no external API, no data leaving your servers. This page covers the whole tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai module, starting where every adoption starts: knowing, before you download gigabytes of weights, whether the machine can handle the model.

How the module was built

The module shipped in slices, and the order below is the recommended reading path -- each section assumes the ones before it. After v0.108 came structured output (v0.142), diarization (v0.223), STT correction (v0.235) and the Coqui runtime behind the [genai-audio] extra (v0.252), all documented in their own sections on this same page. - v0.96: genai.hardware — probing + can_run / recommend. - v0.97: genai.rag — RAG context (SearXNG web search + PDF reading) to inject into LLMs (this page, RAG context). - v0.98: TextGenerator — local LLM + int4/int8 quantization (section Generate text). - v0.99: Embedder, BatchScheduler, ModelRegistry — embeddings + scale (section Embeddings and scale). - v0.102: SpeechToText / TextToSpeech — audio (section Audio (voice)). - v0.107: Ollama backend — OllamaGenerator / OllamaEmbedder, a local LLM without torch (section Ollama backend). - v0.108: long-term memory, AI chat pipeline and vision/tools — ChatMemory / AIChatPipeline (sections Long-term memory and AI chat pipeline).

The [genai] extra (transformers + torch + accelerate) is only needed to run models. The capacity functions import without the extra — torch is only used (when present) to read real GPU VRAM.

docs.title: "Can the machine handle it?"
docs.text:
Loading a too-large model ends in an OOM minutes into the download. can_run answers first:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import can_run

report = can_run(model_id="Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct")

if report.fits:
    print(f"OK on {report.device} — {report.headroom_pct:.0f}% headroom")
else:
    print(report.reason)
    print("Suggestion:", report.suggestion)   # e.g. "Quantize to int4 ..."

CapacityReport carries: fits, device (cuda/mps/cpu), estimated_bytes vs available_bytes, headroom_pct, reason, a concrete suggestion when it doesn't fit (quantize, offload to CPU, or pick a smaller model), and memory_measured, which says whether the device's free memory was actually read (see Without psutil).

Without dtype=, can_run sizes the precision TextGenerator(dtype="auto") loads on the chosen device: bfloat16 on CUDA/MPS, float32 on CPU. Pass dtype= to plan for something else — an explicit dtype= on the generator, or ModelDtypeEnum.INT8/INT4 for quantization=.

Let the SDK pick the precision

recommend(...) tries the native precision of the best available device (bfloat16 on a GPU, float32 on CPU) → int8 → int4 and returns the first config that fits:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import recommend

best = recommend(model_id="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B")
print(best.device, best.dtype, best.fits)   # e.g. cuda int8 True

docs.title: On CPU
docs.text:
Up to 0.303.0 the planner sized every unquantized load at bfloat16, but on CPU TextGenerator loads float32 — twice the bytes. recommend() said "fits" for a model that did not. CPU is now sized at float32, and the rung below it is int8 (never bfloat16, which is not a quantization).

Measured with the GPU hidden (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=), i9-13900F, 62 GB RAM, WSL2, torch 2.14, bitsandbytes 0.50.2, N=3 per row. "Measured" is the process RSS growth from before to after load(), median; transformers 4.57.6 (the floor) / 5.18.0 (the newest on the day):

Model Precision Estimate Measured (4.57.6 / 5.18.0) Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct float32 (was: bfloat16) 2.47 GB (was: 1.24 GB) 2.13 GB / 2.12 GB Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct int8 0.62 GB 0.89 GB / 1.29 GB Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct int4 0.37 GB 1.02 GB / 1.62 GB Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct float32 (was: bfloat16) 15.43 GB (was: 7.71 GB) 12.51 GB / 12.48 GB Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct int8 3.86 GB 3.67 GB / 8.54 GB Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct int4 2.31 GB 3.25 GB / 8.16 GB

What the table says:

  • float32 is what CPU loads, and the new estimate covers the RSS after the load. The peak during the load goes past it: 3.12 GB for the 0.5B and 14.71 GB / 18.66 GB for the 3B.
  • bitsandbytes int8/int4 load and generate on CPU with bitsandbytes 0.50.2 — no error in the table's 24 quantized runs.
  • The quantized estimate can be optimistic. For the 0.5B the measured int4 RSS was 2.7× to 4.4× above it (embeddings are not quantized, and weigh more in a small model). For the 3B on transformers 4.57.6, int8 came in below the estimate (3.67 against 3.86 GB) and int4 above it (3.25 against 2.31 GB). On transformers 5.18.0 the quantized 3B load leaves the process with 5.65 GB of file-backed RSS (RssFile, against 0.36 GB on 4.57.6); the whole process's anonymous memory was 3.33 GB (int8) and 2.95 GB (int4).
  • bitsandbytes on CPU is slower than float32. On the 3B, a generate() capped at 16 tokens took ~9 s at int8/int4 against ~3 s at float32. That is why a CPU quantization suggestion points at the CPU path the SDK already ships:

On CPU, GGUF through Ollama

llama.cpp (build 687e778, -ngl 0, context 4096) serving the Q4_K_M GGUF that Ollama 0.30.11 pulls for qwen2.5:3b sat at 3.60 GB RSS (1.61 GB anonymous + 1.99 GB file-backed) and generated 24 to 27 tokens/s; qwen2.5:0.5b sat at 0.66 GB and 107 to 134 tokens/s (N=3 each). Use OllamaGenerator — memory is in the same range as bitsandbytes int4; the measured advantage is speed. For an agent, what that buys per step (and where it does not: prefill) is in Agents on CPU.

docs.title: Probing the hardware
docs.text:
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import probe_hardware

hw = probe_hardware()
print(hw.cpu_cores, hw.ram_available_bytes)
print(hw.has_cuda, [g.name for g in hw.gpus])   # per-GPU VRAM when CUDA is present

HardwareInfo reports CPU, total/available RAM, CUDA GPUs (name + total/free VRAM), MPS (Apple), and free disk space. Without torch, no GPU shows up (has_cuda=False, gpus=[]). RAM comes from psutil and, on Linux, from /proc/meminfo when psutil is missing — see Without psutil —, bounded by the cgroup in a container with --memory (see In a container with a memory limit). A reading that could not be taken is marked unmeasured, not empty: the RAM fields are 0 with ram_measured=False; when the disk does not answer, disk_free_bytes=0 with disk_measured=False. The fields stay int, so arithmetic on them does not break — but check the flag before reading 0 as "nothing free". A snapshot built by hand (HardwareInfo(...)) has both flags True by default.

docs.title: Environment warnings
docs.text:
HardwareInfo.warnings lists the environment problem the probe can see before a load fails — each item is a sentence with the cause and the fix. An empty list means nothing was detected, not that every load will succeed. Today there is one warning: a CUDA 13 torch build (torch.version.cuda starting with 13.) with CUDA available and faster-whisper's ctranslate2 installed. The ctranslate2 wheels look up libcublas.so.12, and the first transcription with device="cuda" would fail (GPU with [genai-audio]). ctranslate2 is looked up with importlib.util.find_spec, not imported, so the probe loads no CUDA library for it.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import probe_hardware

for warning in probe_hardware().warnings:
    print(warning)

In a python:3.12-slim container with an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, PyPI's torch 2.15.0+cu132 and ctranslate2 4.8.5:

torch is a CUDA 13.2 build, but ctranslate2 (faster-whisper) links against CUDA 12 and looks for libcublas.so.12, which this torch does not install: transcribing on device='cuda' raises 'Library libcublas.so.12 is not found or cannot be loaded' unless the system provides CUDA 12 libraries. Install torch from the CUDA 12 index (https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu126) instead; see 'GPU with [genai-audio]' in the installation docs.

With torch 2.14.1+cu126 from the cu126 index, on the same machine, the list came back empty. The warning cannot see a system-wide CUDA 12 install — which makes the pair work —, which is why the text says "unless the system provides CUDA 12 libraries".

docs.title: Without psutil
docs.text:
psutil ships in the [metrics] extra, not in [genai]. What happens without it depends on the platform:

  • Linux (WSL and containers included): RAM is measured anyway. probe_hardware() reads MemTotal and MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo — the same file psutil reads on Linux. Measured in a clean venv with only the base package (WSL2, 62 GB, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=, no torch): a total of 67,430,916,096 bytes, equal to free -b; MemAvailable within 516 KB of free -b in the same window (the two readings are different instants). Reading the file and calling psutil 7.2.2 in the same process, both byte counts matched exactly. recommend(num_params=500_000_000) gives fits=True at float32.
  • A kernel without MemAvailable (older than 3.14) or with MemAvailable: 0: RAM counts as not measured. psutil estimates in that case; summing MemFree + Buffers + Cached would overstate what a load can claim, and the planner's whole job is not to promise memory that is not there.
  • Windows and macOS: without psutil RAM is not measured, and the report says so in plain words.

In 0.303.1, unmeasured RAM was read as zero free bytes: on the host above, recommend(num_params=500_000_000) returned fits=False at int4 with "Model is too large for this host even quantized; use a smaller model or add memory.". Now, with unknown memory (output below with sys.platform switched to darwin after import, no psutil):

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import recommend

report = recommend(num_params=500_000_000)
print(report.memory_measured, report.fits, report.dtype)
print(report.suggestion)

False False float32
Free RAM was not measured: on darwin measuring RAM requires psutil (pip install 'tempest-fastapi-sdk[metrics]'). Then check again.

On Linux that message only shows up when /proc/meminfo fails too, and it then says that both psutil and /proc/meminfo failed. With unknown memory:

  • fits is False because nothing was verified — an if report.fits: that decides whether to load stays conservative. Code that needs to tell "does not fit" from "don't know" reads memory_measured.
  • dtype is the native precision (float32 on CPU, bfloat16 on MPS), the one TextGenerator(dtype="auto") loads. recommend() does not step down to int8/int4: with no number to compare against, nothing justifies quantizing, and quantizing costs quality and, on CPU, speed (see On CPU).
  • available_bytes and headroom_pct are 0 and carry no information; reason says RAM was not measured.
  • On a GPU the verdict is still measured — VRAM comes from torch/NVML. Only the CPU offload suggestion, which depends on RAM, becomes "RAM was not measured" instead of "the host is too small".

docs.title: In a container with a memory limit
docs.text:
A container's /proc/meminfo shows the host's memory, and psutil.virtual_memory() reads the same file. Up to 0.303.2, in a docker run --memory=512m on a 62 GB host, both reported the host's 67,430,916,096 bytes, and the planner answered fits=True for a 2.5 GB load that does not fit in 512 MiB.

Now, on Linux, probe_hardware() also reads the memory limit of the process's cgroup — memory.max on cgroup v2, memory.limit_in_bytes on v1, found through /proc/self/cgroup and /proc/self/mountinfo, walking up the parent cgroups. When that limit is below the host's RAM it becomes ram_total_bytes, ram_available_bytes becomes the smaller of the host's and what is left in the cgroup, and ram_cgroup_limited=True. It holds with and without psutil:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import can_run, probe_hardware, recommend

info = probe_hardware()
print(info.ram_total_bytes, info.ram_cgroup_limited)

native = can_run(num_params=500_000_000)
print(native.fits, native.dtype)
print(native.reason)

best = recommend(num_params=500_000_000)
print(best.fits, best.dtype)

Output in a python:3.12-slim with --memory=512m (WSL2, Docker 29.6.1, cgroup v2), with this version's wheel and no psutil:

536870912 True
False float32
~2.5 GB needed at float32 exceeds the ~0.4 GB free on cpu. RAM is limited by the container's cgroup to 512 MiB.
True int4

With psutil 7.2.2 installed in the same container the output is the same. Without --memory (memory.max = max) nothing changes: the total stays at the host's 67,430,916,096 bytes and ram_cgroup_limited=False.

How much is left in the cgroup. memory.current (memory.usage_in_bytes on v1) counts page cache, which the kernel drops before it calls the OOM killer. So the math is limit - (usage - (file - shmem)): page cache comes back, but tmpfs/shared memory (shmem) does not, without swap. Measured in the same container with --memory-swap=512m (no swap), allocating 8 MiB at a time until the OOM killer:

Scenario limit - usage limit - (usage - (file - shmem)) Actually allocated 300 MiB of page cache, read once ~183 MiB ~483 MiB 504 MiB the same 300 MiB read 3 times (active_file) ~183 MiB ~483 MiB 504 MiB 300 MiB in /dev/shm (shmem) ~191 MiB ~191 MiB 200 MiB

Subtracting only inactive_file (the docker stats math) would have given ~203 MiB in the second scenario, and subtracting all of file would have given ~491 MiB in the third. With the wheel, probe_hardware() itself reported 417 MiB free and the process allocated 432 MiB (3 out of 3 runs); with 300 MiB of active page cache, it reported 409 MiB and the process allocated 416 or 432 MiB.

Swap is left out

With --memory=512m and no --memory-swap, Docker lets the container use another 512 MiB of swap: on the same host the process allocated 944 MiB before the OOM killer. The planner counts RAM only — a model paged out to swap is not a model that runs.

cgroup v1 is covered by tests over fake files (a limit, the "no limit" sentinel, a /docker/<id> mount root), but it was not measured on a v1 host: Docker on WSL2 uses cgroup v2.

docs.title: Estimate without downloading weights
docs.text:
The math is params × bytes-per-param × overhead. Bytes per param come from the precision (float32=4, float16/bfloat16=2, int8=1, int4≈0.6); the overhead (×1.25) covers activations, KV cache and runtime context.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import estimate_model_bytes, ModelDtypeEnum

gb = estimate_model_bytes(7_000_000_000, ModelDtypeEnum.INT4) / 1e9
print(f"~{gb:.1f} GB")   # 7B in int4

The parameter count can be passed explicitly (num_params=) or read from the Hub by model_id (via huggingface_hub, without downloading the weights — safetensors metadata).

docs.title: Generate text with a local LLM
docs.text:
TextGenerator loads a HuggingFace causal LM once and generates on your hardware. It resolves device and precision itself, supports int4/int8 quantization, loads the weights lazily (on first call), and frees VRAM when idle. Needs [genai] (and [genai-quant] to quantize).

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import TextGenerator

gen = TextGenerator(
    "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct",
    quantization="int4",            # fits a modest GPU; None = full precision
    idle_unload_seconds=300,        # free VRAM after 5 min idle
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    text = await gen.generate("Explain PIX in one sentence.", max_new_tokens=128)

    # chat with a role template:
    reply = await gen.chat([
        {"role": "system", "content": "You answer in English."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is PIX?"},
    ])

    # token-by-token streaming:
    async for piece in gen.stream("Write a haiku about rain."):
        print(piece, end="", flush=True)

    gen.unload()                        # free the memory now


asyncio.run(main())

Weights download once — then it is a disk cache

The first call writes the gigabytes to $HF_HOME/hub (or ~/.cache/huggingface/hub); later runs read them from there, no network. In a container with no volume that is lost on every restart. Pointing the cache somewhere durable, pinning the revision, pre-downloading at deploy time and running offline are all in Model weights ».

Blocking generation runs in asyncio.to_thread — it never blocks the event loop. That holds for stream() too: the first call's load and the wait between tokens happen on a worker thread, and closing the iterator early (a break, a client that disconnected) stops generation at the next token instead of leaving the GPU generating up to max_new_tokens for nobody. Measured with Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER: the first stream used to stall the loop for 4190 ms and now stalls it for 164 to 193 ms (three runs); closing after 5 of 200 tokens used to block for 3532 ms and now returns in ~0.01 ms, with the worker thread done 28 ms later.

device="auto" picks CUDA → MPS → CPU; dtype="auto" uses bf16 on GPU and fp32 on CPU.

Check before loading

Pair it with the capacity check: run can_run / recommend to pick a quantization/device that fits before instantiating the TextGenerator.

Free VRAM between bursts

With idle_unload_seconds set, call gen.unload_if_idle() periodically (e.g. in a @tq.interval(60) TaskQueue task) — it unloads only once past the idle threshold, no background-thread magic. unload() frees immediately.

A call in progress does not count as idle: seconds_idle reads 0.0 while it runs and unload_if_idle() returns False. An unload() that arrives mid-call (including one from a ModelRegistry eviction) waits: whichever call finishes last drops the weights. And several simultaneous first calls load the model once. The same holds for every local loader (Embedder, Reranker, ImageGenerator, SpeechToText, TextToSpeech, SpeakerDiarizer, VoiceEmbedder, OnnxEmbedder...) and for the face recognition FaceRecognizer.

docs.title: Several requests at once on CPU: max_concurrent
docs.text:
Every call runs on a worker thread, and on CPU the model.generate of one thread already uses torch's whole intra-op pool. With no limit, four agents answering at once become four threads fighting over the same cores: nobody finishes early, and everybody finishes late. max_concurrent queues the extra requests instead:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import TextGenerator

gen = TextGenerator(
    "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
    device="cpu",
    max_concurrent=1,               # one decode at a time; the rest wait in line
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    replies = await asyncio.gather(
        *(gen.generate(f"Give a Python tip, number {n}.") for n in range(4))
    )
    for reply in replies:
        print(reply)


asyncio.run(main())

Measured with Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on CPU (WSL2 on an i9-13900F, 12 visible logical CPUs = 6 cores × 2, torch 2.14 with 6 intra-op threads), 128 forced tokens (min_new_tokens = max_new_tokens), do_sample=False, each configuration in its own process, median of 5 rounds:

Concurrent calls max_concurrent Throughput Median latency Max latency 1 None 28.3 tokens/s 4.53 s 4.53 s 2 None 24.6 tokens/s 10.26 s 10.42 s 2 1 26.7 tokens/s 7.27 s 9.60 s 2 2 27.7 tokens/s 9.13 s 9.24 s 4 None 22.4 tokens/s 22.73 s 22.85 s 4 1 26.9 tokens/s 11.91 s 19.03 s 4 2 25.6 tokens/s 14.80 s 19.97 s

With four requests and max_concurrent=1, throughput is back to 95% of a lone call's, the median latency halves, and the last one still finishes earlier than it would with no limit. A lone call does not change: over two re-runs of 9 rounds, 4.56 s against 4.57 s and 4.66 s against 4.65 s.

Why a queue of dedicated threads, and not a semaphore

Torch's OpenMP runtime keeps one worker team per thread that calls the model, and asyncio's default executor hands each call to whichever of its threads is free. Measured on the same hardware, decoding strictly one at a time: 4.5 s per call while everything ran on the same thread, 6.4 s per call after alternating across four live threads — each new thread added 6 threads to the process, and the slowdown stayed even after going back to the first one. A semaphore in front of the default executor serialized calls and made each one slower: four concurrent calls finished at 18.5 tokens/s, below the 22.8 with no limit at all measured in the same process. That is why max_concurrent=N builds a pool of N threads owned by the generator, and decoding never leaves them. (OMP_WAIT_POLICY=PASSIVE does not fix it: it put the lone call at 6.7 s.)

The default stays None (no limit, every call starts right away), so an SDK upgrade does not change anyone's concurrency — the trade-off was not measured on GPU. On CPU, start with max_concurrent=1. A request cancelled while waiting in line leaves it without running; one cancelled while decoding stops at the next token and only frees its place once the thread has really finished. It covers generate, chat, chat_with_tools, generate_structured, chat_structured and stream (which holds its place until the last token, or until one token after you close the iterator). VisionTextGenerator takes the same max_concurrent=.

What about the thread count?

There is no thread knob on TextGenerator, on purpose: torch.set_num_threads is process-wide, not per generator, and torch's default here was already the number of visible physical cores (6). With max_concurrent=1 the throughput under load stayed within 5% of a lone call's, so there was little left to gain. If you need to change it, call torch.set_num_threads(n) once at startup, knowing it applies to every model in the process.

docs.title: Hosted backend (DeepSeek, Groq, OpenRouter, vLLM...)
docs.text:
Anthropic, OpenAI and DeepSeek

This section covers OpenAICompatGenerator itself. For Claude (AnthropicGenerator), tool calling, structured output, embeddings, settings (HostedGenAISettings) and typed errors, see Hosted generative AI.

Not every service wants to hold weights: sometimes the budget that matters is cost per token, not RAM. OpenAI's /chat/completions format became the common denominator — DeepSeek, Groq, Together, OpenRouter, Mistral, vLLM's server, TGI's OpenAI route and Azure all speak it — so one client reaches all of them by swapping base_url and model.

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OpenAICompatGenerator

gen = OpenAICompatGenerator(
    "deepseek-flash",
    api_key="sk-...",                        # never hardcoded: read it from settings
    base_url="https://api.deepseek.com",
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    text: str = await gen.generate("Explain PIX in one sentence.")
    print(text)


asyncio.run(main())

It satisfies TextBackend, so it drops into make_genai_router and AIChatPipeline in place of TextGenerator or OllamaGenerator with no other change. An empty key raises ValueError at construction — the mistake is a configuration one, and it surfaces where the configuration is read rather than as a 401 inside the first background job.

docs.title: What the call cost
docs.text:
generate_with_usage returns the text and the usage the provider itself reported. That is the number being billed, so it is the one worth persisting when you need per-user accounting — not a local re-count with a different tokenizer:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OpenAICompatGenerator, TokenUsage

gen = OpenAICompatGenerator(
    "deepseek-flash",
    api_key="sk-...",
    base_url="https://api.deepseek.com",
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    text: str
    usage: TokenUsage | None = None
    text, usage = await gen.generate_with_usage("Summarize this.", system="Be brief.")
    if usage is not None:
        print(usage.input_tokens, usage.output_tokens, usage.total_tokens)


asyncio.run(main())

TokenUsage adds with +, for a job made of several calls (a map-reduce summary is N chunk calls plus one reduce call, and what you want to record is the job, not each leg).

None is not zero

usage is None means "the provider did not say", which differs from a zeroed usage claiming the call was free. Code that persists usage should write no row in that case.

total comes from the provider, not from the sum

No provider is obliged to bill input + output: cached-prefix discounts show up exactly that way. The reported total is the authority; the sum is only a fallback when the field is absent.

docs.title: The prefix that came from cache
docs.text:
When the start of a prompt matches a recent call, the provider serves that part from cache and bills it far cheaper — DeepSeek's table puts the hit token two orders of magnitude below the miss token. cache_hit_tokens is that slice:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OpenAICompatGenerator, TokenUsage

gen = OpenAICompatGenerator(
    "deepseek-flash",
    api_key="sk-...",
    base_url="https://api.deepseek.com",
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    usage: TokenUsage | None
    _text, usage = await gen.generate_with_usage("Summarize this.")
    if usage is not None:
        print(usage.input_tokens, "in, of which", usage.cache_hit_tokens, "cached")


asyncio.run(main())

It is a slice of input_tokens, not an extra charge

cache_hit_tokens counts tokens already inside input_tokens. Adding the two bills the prefix twice. Pricing subtracts instead: (input − cached) × normal_rate + cached × cached_rate, which is what AIUsageStore.estimate_cost does.

Two spellings, both read

The same OpenAI-compatible family writes this two ways: DeepSeek sends prompt_cache_hit_tokens at the root of usage, OpenAI sends prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens. from_payload reads both — handling only one works against the provider you tested and quietly overcharges on the other.

A provider with no prompt cache sends no field at all, and the slice is 0. Zero is honest here (nothing came from cache), unlike a missing usage as a whole, which is None.

docs.title: Provider-specific fields: extra_body
docs.text:
The format is shared; the extensions are not. extra_body is merged into every request body, under the computed fields — so it cannot accidentally redirect the call to another model.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OpenAICompatGenerator

gen = OpenAICompatGenerator(
    "deepseek-flash",
    api_key="sk-...",
    base_url="https://api.deepseek.com",
    extra_body={"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}},
)

A hybrid reasoning model returns empty content

That thinking field is not decoration. A hybrid model with reasoning on by default spends max_tokens on the hidden chain before the real content — billed as normal output — so a budget sized for the answer is exhausted there and content comes back empty. Reported by a service that hit it against DeepSeek; this repo does not reproduce it against a live provider. Turning it off is cheaper and safer, not a quality loss, when you only want the result.

HuggingFace-only fields stay off the wire

do_sample, top_k and repetition_penalty exist on GenerationConfig but not in the OpenAI format, and a strict provider refuses the body (an audit reported 400 from OpenAI; the tests here use a mock transport). So they are dropped; do_sample=False without an explicit temperature becomes temperature=0. A provider that accepts those names (vLLM's server documents top_k and repetition_penalty) is opted in with forward_params=["top_k", "repetition_penalty"]. And model, messages and stream cannot arrive as a generation keyword — generate("hi", model="other") raises TypeError instead of redirecting the call.

docs.title: Ollama backend
docs.text:
TextGenerator loads HuggingFace weights with torch on your hardware — great when you have GPU/torch, but it means downloading gigabytes of weights and managing VRAM. If you already run a local Ollama daemon, OllamaGenerator uses the same genai surface (router, Retriever, GenerationConfig) talking HTTP to Ollama: no torch, no local weights, no load(). Ollama handles the download and VRAM for you.

Needs the [genai-ollama] extra (just httpx) and the daemon running with the model already pulled:

uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[genai-ollama]"
ollama pull llama3.2
ollama pull nomic-embed-text

Ollama also speaks and transcribes

Since v0.40.11 Ollama generates speech (/v1/audio/speech) and lfm3-audio transcribes; OllamaSpeech wraps both. What was measured, the limits and the sources are in Voice through Ollama.

docs.title: Generate text via Ollama
docs.text:
OllamaGenerator mirrors TextGenerator — generate, chat and stream, same signature:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OllamaGenerator

gen = OllamaGenerator("llama3.2")   # default base_url = http://127.0.0.1:11434


async def main() -> None:
    # simple generation:
    text = await gen.generate("Explain PIX in one sentence.")
    print(text)

    # chat with a role template:
    reply = await gen.chat([
        {"role": "system", "content": "You answer in English."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is PIX?"},
    ])
    print(reply)

    # token-by-token streaming:
    async for piece in gen.stream("Write a haiku about rain."):
        print(piece, end="", flush=True)


asyncio.run(main())

No load() or unload(): the model lives in the Ollama daemon, which pulls it on the first call and frees VRAM on its own. base_url points at another host when Ollama isn't local (the default is DEFAULT_OLLAMA_URL); keep_alive, timeout and your own http_client (to reuse the pool) are optional.

A read timeout is not retried

The HTTPClient the generator builds retries a connection error and a retryable status (429, 5xx), but not a ReadTimeout. When the client stops waiting, the daemon aborts the generation — in the Ollama 0.30.11 log each attempt shows up as a 500 of exactly the timeout — so the next attempt starts from zero and times out again. Measured with qwen2.5:3b on CPU (options={"num_gpu": 0}) and timeout=10: up to v0.303.1 the failure arrived after 31.5 s, after three aborts; now it arrives after 10.0 s, with one (median of N=3 before and N=5 after). The same holds for OllamaEmbedder and OpenAICompatGenerator. To get the retry back, pass the policy explicitly — it is used as given:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import RetryPolicy
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OllamaGenerator

gen: OllamaGenerator = OllamaGenerator(
    "llama3.2",
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(retry_on_read_timeout=True),
)

GenerationConfig maps to Ollama options

The same typed GenerationConfig works here — its fields are translated to Ollama options: max_new_tokens→num_predict, repetition_penalty→repeat_penalty, and temperature/top_p/top_k/ seed/stop pass through. do_sample=False becomes temperature=0 (greedy generation).

A daemon error raises OllamaError

Ollama reports some failures (model not pulled, a runner that crashed mid-way) as an {"error": "..."} body — on a 200 or as one line of the NDJSON stream. generate, chat, embed and the structured variants raise OllamaError (with .model and .detail) instead of returning "", and stream raises on the error line instead of ending as if it had finished — pieces already yielded stay yielded.

chat follows generate on cache and metrics: with generation_cache=, a repeated deterministic call skips the daemon, and with metrics= it is recorded under the chat operation with Ollama's token counts. The chat key is scoped apart from generate, so a prompt equal to the serialized messages never collides.

docs.title: Context window: num_ctx
docs.text:
Ollama processes at most num_ctx prompt tokens, and it cuts the rest without a word: the reply comes back 200, no error, generated over a slice of what you sent. Measured on Ollama 0.30.11 (lfm2.5-thinking:1.2b, on a 16 GB RTX 4070 Ti SUPER): a 35,018-token chat came back with prompt_eval_count 2,051 under the default, and 35,018 with num_ctx=65536. Pin the window on the generator, and it goes with every call:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import GenerationConfig, OllamaGenerator

gen = OllamaGenerator(
    "llama3.2",
    num_ctx=32768,
    options={"num_thread": 8},
    config=GenerationConfig(max_new_tokens=512),
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    reply: str = await gen.chat([{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}])
    print(reply)


asyncio.run(main())
  • num_ctx becomes the num_ctx option of every request.
  • options are raw Ollama options (num_thread, num_gpu, …), also on every request. num_ctx in both places raises ValueError.
  • config is the default GenerationConfig. Each call's own wins field by field, and the call's **kwargs win over everything.

This matters most for a caller that passes no option per call — the agent loop is one. The window and the default config are part of the generation_cache key, so two generators with different defaults never answer from each other's cache.

docs.title: Embeddings via Ollama + RAG
docs.text:
OllamaEmbedder satisfies the same SupportsEmbed protocol as Embedder, so it drops into Retriever and the /embed endpoint with nothing else to change — the embeddings come from Ollama instead of torch:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OllamaEmbedder, OllamaGenerator
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import InMemoryVectorStore, PdfReader, Retriever

gen = OllamaGenerator("llama3.2")
rag = Retriever(OllamaEmbedder("nomic-embed-text"), InMemoryVectorStore())


async def main() -> None:
    await rag.index(PdfReader().chunks("/kb/manual.pdf"))     # once
    context = await rag.retrieve("how to refund?", top_k=5)   # cheap, afterwards
    print(await gen.generate(context))


asyncio.run(main())

embed(texts, *, batch_size=32) returns list[list[float]], just like Embedder.

docs.title: Hybrid search (BM25 + dense)
docs.text:
Dense search captures meaning but misses exact terms — proper nouns, codes, acronyms a query shares verbatim with a chunk. Sparse BM25 nails those and ignores semantics. HybridRetriever runs both over the same indexed chunks and fuses their rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion — so "what does BACEN do?" finds the chunk that says "BACEN" even when the dense score is lukewarm. BM25 comes from rank-bm25 (the [genai-rag] extra).

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import Embedder
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import (
    HybridRetriever,
    InMemoryVectorStore,
    chunk_text,
)

rag = HybridRetriever(
    Embedder("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", normalize=True),
    InMemoryVectorStore(),
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    chunks = chunk_text(
        "The CNPJ identifies a legal entity at the Receita Federal.",
        source="faq.md",
    )
    await rag.index(chunks)                           # indexes dense + BM25
    hits = await rag.search("what is CNPJ?", top_k=5)  # fuses dense + sparse
    print(hits)


asyncio.run(main())

search(query, top_k, candidates) takes candidates from each side and fuses to top_k. reciprocal_rank_fusion(rankings, k=60) is exposed standalone to fuse arbitrary rankings. The BM25 index is in-memory (rebuilt on each index) — good up to a few tens of thousands of chunks. It also has retrieve(query, top_k) (hybrid search → context block), so HybridRetriever satisfies SupportsRetrieve and drops into make_genai_router(retriever=...) in place of a Retriever.

Each index replaces the sources it names

A chunk is identified by (source, index, text) — not by (source, index) alone, which chunk_text repeats on every call (it restarts index at 0). And each index(chunks) replaces whatever was already indexed for the batch's sources: re-indexing an edited document leaves neither the old version nor a tail of it answering searches. So pass every chunk of a source in the same call. InMemoryVectorStore, PgVectorStore and ChromaVectorStore apply the same replacement on the dense side; a VectorStore of your own that only appends keeps returning the old rows, and HybridRetriever drops them before fusion (they only cost candidates slots).

On the sparse side, only chunks sharing at least one term with the query enter the fusion. With no overlap BM25 scores every chunk 0, and a list of zeros "sorted by score" is just insertion order — added into RRF, it inverted the dense ranking.

docs.title: Reranking (cross-encoder)
docs.text:
Dense search (embed the query, embed the chunks, cosine) is fast but coarse: it never sees query and chunk together. A cross-encoder scores each (query, chunk) pair jointly — too slow for the whole corpus, ideal as a second stage over the top-N candidates. Inject a Reranker into the Retriever: search over-fetches candidates from the store and the cross-encoder narrows them to top_k.

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import Embedder
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import InMemoryVectorStore, Reranker, Retriever

rag = Retriever(
    Embedder("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", normalize=True),
    InMemoryVectorStore(),
    reranker=Reranker("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2"),
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    # search fetches max(top_k, rerank_candidates) from the store, then reorders:
    chunks = await rag.search("how to refund?", top_k=5, rerank_candidates=20)


asyncio.run(main())

Without a reranker the Retriever stays dense-only. Reranker (the [genai] extra) has lazy load + unload/unload_if_idle like TextGenerator.

docs.title: Same router, torch OR Ollama
docs.text:
make_genai_router type-hints TextBackend / SupportsEmbed, so the Ollama objects slot in where the torch ones went without touching anything else:

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import (
    OllamaEmbedder,
    OllamaGenerator,
    make_genai_router,
)

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(
    make_genai_router(
        text_generator=OllamaGenerator("llama3.2"),
        embedder=OllamaEmbedder("nomic-embed-text"),
    )
)

Swapping TextGenerator / Embedder (torch) for OllamaGenerator / OllamaEmbedder is the only change — the /generate, /generate/stream, /chat and /embed endpoints are identical.

TextBackend is the seam for any engine

TextBackend is a runtime_checkable Protocol (generate / chat / stream). Ollama is just one implementation; to plug in vLLM, TGI or a hosted API, implement the same protocol and inject it into the router / Retriever — the call site doesn't change.

docs.title: Long-term memory
docs.text:
A chat that forgets everything between sessions isn't an assistant — it's a form. ChatMemory gives the conversation long-term memory: every turn becomes an indexed embedding, and before answering you recall the most relevant snippets from that same user — even from old chats. Recall is recency-aware: what is semantically close and recent floats to the top.

Needs the [genai-chroma] extra (ChromaDB) — if the service already runs Postgres, see Memory in Postgres with pgvector, which does without it. The embedder is any SupportsEmbed — here an OllamaEmbedder, no torch:

import asyncio
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OllamaEmbedder
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import ChatMemory

memory = ChatMemory(
    OllamaEmbedder("nomic-embed-text"),
    persist_directory="./chat_memory",   # None = in-memory only
    top_k=5,
    min_similarity=0.55,
)


async def main() -> None:
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    # index two turns of an old conversation:
    await memory.index(
        user_id="u1", chat_id="c1", message_id="m1",
        role="user", content="I prefer short, direct answers.",
        created_at=now,
    )
    await memory.index(
        user_id="u1", chat_id="c1", message_id="m2",
        role="user", content="I work with FastAPI and Postgres.",
        created_at=now,
    )

    # in a NEW chat, recall what matters for that user:
    hits = await memory.search(
        user_id="u1",
        query="Which framework and database does he work with?",
        exclude_chat_id="c2",     # ignore the current chat
    )
    for hit in hits:
        print(f"{hit.score:.2f}  {hit.content}")


asyncio.run(main())

0.58  I work with FastAPI and Postgres.

Only one memory comes back. Against this query, "I prefer short, direct answers." scores 0.388 similarity, below the 0.55 floor, and is dropped before the re-rank. The floor decides what reaches the model: a vague query such as "what stack does he use?" scores 0.429 against the right text and recalls nothing (measured with nomic-embed-text). Calibrate min_similarity with your product's real queries, not the example's.

search filters by user_id, applies the similarity floor (min_similarity), then blends in the recency decay — each MemoryHit carries content, role, chat_id, created_at, similarity (raw cosine) and score (the final value, recency included).

Every user shares one collection, so every mutation names its owner. delete_for_chat(user_id=..., chat_id=...) deletes that user's rows for the chat when they remove it — the chat_id comes from the request body and can repeat across users, and the other users' rows stay. delete_for_user(user_id=...) erases a user's whole memory (account deletion). And index refuses, with ValueError, a message_id that already belongs to another user instead of overwriting that user's row.

Chroma is asked for the top_k * candidate_multiplier nearest neighbours (default 4), and the recency re-rank picks top_k of them — so a recent message ranked just below the raw top-K can still rise. With candidate_multiplier=1 only the raw top-K is reordered. The per-user quota (max_entries_per_user) evicts the oldest UTC instant first: created_at is stored converted to UTC, alongside a created_at_ts in epoch seconds, and older rows without that field are ordered by parsing the ISO string. Sorting the ISO strings put 10:00+05:00 after 08:00+00:00, although it is three hours earlier.

The [genai-chroma] extra and the recency decay

Install with uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[genai-chroma]". The final score combines similarity and recency via (1 - recency_weight) * sim + recency_weight * sim * decay, with decay = 0.5 ** (age_in_days / recency_halflife_days). With the defaults (14 days, recency_weight=0.5), a 14-day-old snippet has decay = 0.5 and scores 0.75 of its similarity, against 1.0 for a freshly written one of equal similarity. recency_weight=0 = similarity only.

Generic RAG with ChromaVectorStore

Just need a persistent vector store (without the per-user memory logic)? ChromaVectorStore is a VectorStore like the others — add(chunks, vectors) / search(vector, top_k=) — backed by ChromaDB, with the same re-index rule as the other stores (add replaces the batch's sources). Drop it into Retriever in place of InMemoryVectorStore / PgVectorStore to get a disk-persisted corpus:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OllamaEmbedder
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import ChromaVectorStore, Retriever

rag = Retriever(
    OllamaEmbedder("nomic-embed-text"),
    ChromaVectorStore(collection_name="kb", persist_directory="./kb"),
)

docs.title: Memory in Postgres with pgvector
docs.text:
Does your service already run Postgres? Then ChromaDB is a second database: outside the application's backups and outside its transactions — deleting a conversation and its memory stops being atomic. PgChatMemory is the same memory in a pgvector table of the database you already have: same methods (index, search, delete_for_chat, delete_for_user), same parameters and the same ranking (similarity floor, recency re-rank, over-fetch, per-user quota).

It does not need the [genai-chroma] extra nor the pgvector package: the vector travels as text and Postgres casts it. All it takes is the async driver ([postgres], which brings asyncpg) and the vector extension on the server.

Switching backends means switching the class — the rest of the code stays the same:

import asyncio
from datetime import UTC, datetime

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OllamaEmbedder
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import PgChatMemory

db = AsyncDatabaseManager("postgresql+asyncpg://app:app@localhost:5432/app")
memory = PgChatMemory(
    OllamaEmbedder("nomic-embed-text"),
    db,
    dim=768,                 # the embedder's vector size
    table="chat_memory",
)


async def main() -> None:
    await db.connect()
    await memory.ensure_schema()   # CREATE EXTENSION + table + indexes

    await memory.index(
        user_id="u1", chat_id="c1", message_id="m1",
        role="user", content="Trabalho com FastAPI e Postgres.",
        created_at=datetime.now(UTC),
    )
    hits = await memory.search(
        user_id="u1",
        query="Com que framework e banco ele trabalha?",
        exclude_chat_id="c2",
    )
    for hit in hits:
        print(f"{hit.score:.2f}  {hit.content}")

    await db.disconnect()


asyncio.run(main())

With nomic-embed-text (which produces 768-dimension vectors) on a local Ollama and pgvector/pgvector:pg17, this prints:

0.68  Trabalho com FastAPI e Postgres.

Every search is WHERE user_id = :user_id (plus chat_id <> :exclude_chat_id when you pass exclude_chat_id) before ordering by the cosine distance <=> — one user's memory never shows up for another. message_id is the primary key: indexing the same message again replaces the row, and a message_id that already belongs to another user is refused with ValueError.

docs.title: Delete the conversation and its memory in one transaction
docs.text:
delete_for_chat and delete_for_user accept your session. When you pass it, the DELETE joins your transaction: if the rest fails, the memory comes back with it.

from sqlalchemy import text

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import PgChatMemory


async def delete_chat(
    db: AsyncDatabaseManager,
    memory: PgChatMemory,
    *,
    user_id: str,
    chat_id: str,
) -> None:
    async with db.transaction() as session:
        await session.execute(
            text("DELETE FROM chats WHERE id = :id AND owner_id = :owner"),
            {"id": chat_id, "owner": user_id},
        )
        await memory.delete_for_chat(
            user_id=user_id, chat_id=chat_id, session=session,
        )

Without session, each delete opens and commits a session of its own.

docs.title: The vector extension on the server
docs.text:
ensure_schema() runs CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector, so Postgres must have the extension installed and the application role must be allowed to create it (otherwise run CREATE EXTENSION vector once as a superuser before starting the service).

The official postgres:*-alpine image does not ship pgvector

On postgres:17-alpine, CREATE EXTENSION vector fails with:

ERROR:  extension "vector" is not available
DETAIL:  Could not open extension control file "/usr/local/share/postgresql/extension/vector.control": No such file or directory.
HINT:  The extension must first be installed on the system where PostgreSQL is running.

Use an image that already ships the extension, such as pgvector/pgvector:pg17:

services:
  db:
    image: pgvector/pgvector:pg17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"

docs.title: HNSW index (optional)
docs.text:
Without an approximate index the search is exact: the (user_id, created_at) B-tree finds the user's rows and Postgres sorts only those. At a typical user's volume, that is enough. For large tables, ensure_schema(ann_index="hnsw") builds the HNSW index (vector_cosine_ops), the same one PgVectorStore builds.

HNSW with a per-user filter needs pgvector 0.8.0+

The HNSW index returns at most hnsw.ef_search rows (of any user) and the user_id filter runs afterwards. Measured on pgvector 0.8.6, with 50 000 rows and a user owning 500 of them, the plan used HNSW and that user's search came back empty. Since 0.8.0 pgvector has iterative index scans: search turns on hnsw.iterative_scan in its own transaction, and the same search returns its 5 hits. That is why ensure_schema(ann_index=...) refuses an older pgvector with RuntimeError — without an approximate index, the exact search works on any version.

docs.title: AI chat pipeline
docs.text:
Here the earlier slices click together. Building a "real" chatbot — memory, web RAG, tool-calling, optional TTS — usually means writing (and maintaining) an entire inference microservice. AIChatPipeline does it inside your process: you inject the pieces you've already seen (OllamaGenerator, ChatMemory, WebSearch, Tools) and call respond.

Picking the chat's voice model

TTS weight licences vary more than they look (F5-TTS and AudioLDM 2 are non-commercial). Measured table and sources in Picking a voice or audio model.

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import HTTPClient
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import (
    AIChatPipeline,
    OllamaEmbedder,
    OllamaGenerator,
    Tool,
)
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import ChatMemory, SearxngBackend, WebSearch


async def get_weather(args: dict) -> str:
    """Tool handler: takes validated args, returns text for the model."""
    return f"It's 24°C in {args['city']}."


weather_tool = Tool(
    name="get_weather",
    description="Look up the weather for a city.",
    parameters={
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["city"],
    },
    handler=get_weather,
)

pipeline = AIChatPipeline(
    OllamaGenerator("llama3.2"),
    memory=ChatMemory(OllamaEmbedder("nomic-embed-text")),
    web_search=WebSearch(SearxngBackend("http://localhost:8080", http_client=HTTPClient())),
    tools=[weather_tool],
    base_system_prompt="You are a concise assistant. Answer in English.",
)


async def main() -> None:
    result = await pipeline.respond(
        user_id="u1",
        chat_id="c1",
        content="What's the weather in Recife?",
        use_web_search=False,      # True augments the prompt with web search
        speak=False,               # True generates audio (needs tts=)
    )
    print(result.reply)
    print("tools called:", result.tool_calls_made)
    print("sources:", result.sources)
    print("memories used:", len(result.memory_hits))


asyncio.run(main())

respond runs the whole cycle: recall memory → (optional) augment with web search → build the messages (system + memory + context + history + user turn; images ride on the user turn) → generate (with a bounded tool-calling loop when tools + a capable backend are set — OllamaGenerator or the local TextGenerator (transformers); otherwise plain chat) → (optional) TTS → best-effort index of both turns.

Moderation + context window in the pipeline

Optional constructor args: moderator= (a ModerationBackend — RuleModerator/ClassifierModerator) screens the input and every history turn before generating and the reply after — in respond and in stream; a flagged turn answers blocked_message (a flagged input never calls the model). tokenizer= + max_context_tokens= trim the oldest turns (via truncate_messages) to fit the window before generating. Both opt-in.

AIChatResult carries reply, sources, memory_hits, tool_calls_made and audio_base64.

Tools on the local backend (transformers)

TextGenerator.chat_with_tools renders the chat template with tools= (transformers >= 4.44) and parses the tool calls the model emits (<tool_call>{...}</tool_call> for Qwen/Hermes, or Llama JSON), returning the same shape as OllamaGenerator — so the same AIChatPipeline runs on local weights, no daemon required. Use a tool-capable instruct model (e.g. Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct).

docs.title: Ready endpoint: make_ai_chat_router
docs.text:
One router, a whole chat backend in-process:

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import (
    AIChatPipeline,
    TextGenerator,
    TextModelEnum,
    make_ai_chat_router,
)

pipeline = AIChatPipeline(generator=TextGenerator(TextModelEnum.QWEN2_5_7B_INSTRUCT))


app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(make_ai_chat_router(pipeline))   # prefix /api/ai-chat

It mounts POST /api/ai-chat/chat (returns AIChatResult) and POST /api/ai-chat/chat/stream (tokens over SSE). The body is {"chat_id": ..., "content": ..., "history": [...]} — no user_id.

The router is stateless

History lives in the request body, not on the server — each call sends history. That keeps the backend sessionless (horizontal scale for free) and long-term memory handles the "remembering" via ChatMemory.

docs.title: With memory: the conversation owner comes from the session
docs.text:
With memory= on the pipeline, every turn recalls and indexes the user's memories. Who the user is comes from your auth dependency, never from the body:

# src/api/app.py

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import (
    AIChatPipeline,
    OllamaEmbedder,
    OllamaGenerator,
    make_ai_chat_router,
)
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai.rag import ChatMemory

from src.api.dependencies.auth import current_user_id

pipeline = AIChatPipeline(
    OllamaGenerator("llama3.2"),
    memory=ChatMemory(OllamaEmbedder("nomic-embed-text")),
)


def create_app() -> FastAPI:
    """Mount the AI chat behind the service's own auth."""
    app = FastAPI()
    app.include_router(
        make_ai_chat_router(
            pipeline,
            current_user_id=current_user_id,
            dependencies=[Depends(current_user_id)],
        ),
    )
    return app

current_user_id is required alongside memory

Recalling memory under a user_id taken from the body would hand anyone's past conversations to whoever knows their id — and AIChatResult returns the memory_hits. So the router refuses that combination at mount time (ValueError). Without memory, current_user_id is optional and the turn runs with no owner.

The body does not pick roles

history[].role accepts only "user" and "assistant". A client-sent "system" turn would sit in the prompt with the authority of your base_system_prompt — the body gets a 422. And with moderator=, every history turn's content goes through the same filter as the new message.

Migrating from a version that read user_id from the body

Up to 0.299.0, AIChatRequestSchema had user_id and the router passed it to memory.search. Now:

  • the field is gone from the schema; an older client still sending user_id does not break — the value is ignored;
  • a pipeline with memory= needs current_user_id= on make_ai_chat_router, or mounting raises ValueError;
  • history with a role other than user/assistant now answers 422;
  • calling the pipeline directly, user_id=None skips memory for the turn (no recall, no indexing).

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
stream yields tokens as they come (prompt mode; it resolves any tool-calls before it starts emitting):

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import AIChatPipeline, TextGenerator, TextModelEnum

pipeline = AIChatPipeline(generator=TextGenerator(TextModelEnum.QWEN2_5_7B_INSTRUCT))


async def stream_demo() -> None:
    async for token in pipeline.stream(
        user_id="u1", chat_id="c1", content="Explain RAG in one sentence.",
    ):
        print(token, end="", flush=True)


asyncio.run(stream_demo())

Moderation while streaming: what was sent stays sent

With moderator=, stream screens the reply too, and stream_moderation= on the constructor picks how:

  • "incremental" (default) — before each piece is sent, the text generated so far (that piece included) goes through the moderator. On the first flag the stream stops and the last piece is blocked_message. Earlier pieces were already delivered and cannot be recalled; the guarantee is that the piece which makes the text flaggable is never sent. With RuleModerator and the block list ["secret"], the reply "here is the SECRET plan", emitted one character per piece, comes out as "here is the SECRE" followed by blocked_message — the term is never emitted whole, a prefix of it can be. It costs one moderator call per piece.
  • "buffered" — generates the whole reply, moderates once, and only then sends: either the whole reply as a single piece, or blocked_message. Nothing leaks, but the client waits for the full generation. It is the choice for a ClassifierModerator, which would cost one inference per piece in incremental mode.

A blocked reply is not indexed into memory, same as respond.

The inference microservice becomes a choice, not a requirement

With the pipeline in-process, running a separate LLM-only service turns into an organizational decision (isolate the GPU, scale it apart) — not an architectural obligation. The same TextBackend lets you swap Ollama for vLLM/TGI later without touching the call site.

docs.title: Generate embeddings
docs.text:
Embedder turns text into vectors on your hardware (semantic search, RAG, clustering). It loads the model once, batches, and (optionally) caches a vector per text — a cache hit never touches the model.

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import Embedder, InMemoryEmbeddingCache

emb = Embedder(
    "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
    cache=InMemoryEmbeddingCache(),     # or a Redis wrapper (get/set)
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    vectors = await emb.embed(["what is pix?", "how to refund?"])   # list[list[float]]


asyncio.run(main())

cache is any object with get(key)->list|None and set(key, val) — pass a wrapper over AsyncRedisManager to share across workers. InMemoryEmbeddingCache is an LRU of 1024 vectors by default (max_entries=; None removes the bound), so a long-lived worker does not grow forever. device/dtype/unload/unload_if_idle work as on TextGenerator.

For semantic search, use normalize=True (unit vectors) + the cosine_similarity function:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import Embedder, cosine_similarity


emb = Embedder("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2", normalize=True)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    q, *docs = await emb.embed(["question", "doc a", "doc b"])
    ranked = sorted(docs, key=lambda d: cosine_similarity(q, d), reverse=True)


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: ONNX embeddings (no torch)
docs.text:
When you don't want the heavy torch/transformers stack just to embed, OnnxEmbedder runs an embedding model exported to ONNX via ONNX Runtime — light dependencies (onnxruntime + tokenizers, the [genai-onnx] extra), cheap on CPU. It satisfies the same SupportsEmbed, so it drops into a Retriever / make_genai_router unchanged.

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import OnnxEmbedder

emb = OnnxEmbedder(
    "all-MiniLM-L6-v2.onnx",
    tokenizer="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
    normalize=True,
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    vectors = await emb.embed(["question", "doc a"])


asyncio.run(main())

The default pooling is the attention-mask-weighted mean of the token embeddings (not a naive average over padding), so vectors match the torch Embedder for the same model (cosine ≈ 1.0). BGE-family models are trained on the [CLS] token — pass pooling="cls" for them, as the model card says. A graph exported with its pooling head baked in (a 2-D sentence_embedding output) is used as is, and padding uses the tokenizer's own <pad> (id 1 in RoBERTa/XLM-R), not the id 0 tokenizers assumes. Export the model in a throwaway environment — optimum is not a dependency of this package, because it pins transformers<4.58 in the lock of whoever installs it:

uvx --from "optimum[onnxruntime]" optimum-cli export onnx \
    --model sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 \
    --task feature-extraction exports/minilm

Then point model_path at the generated .onnx.

docs.title: Batch concurrent inference
docs.text:
On a GPU, one item at a time wastes the device. BatchScheduler coalesces concurrent calls into a single batch — each caller still awaits its own result:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import BatchScheduler, Embedder, EmbeddingModelEnum

emb = Embedder(EmbeddingModelEnum.ALL_MINILM_L6_V2)


async def embed_batch(texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Embed a whole batch in one forward pass."""
    return await emb.embed(texts)


sched = BatchScheduler(embed_batch, max_batch=32, max_wait_ms=10)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    # N concurrent requests become 1 forward pass:
    vector = await sched.submit("text")
    await sched.aclose()


asyncio.run(main())

It forms a batch once max_batch items are queued or max_wait_ms has elapsed since the first — whichever comes first. A handler error propagates to every caller in that batch.

Every path resolves every caller: a handler that returns something without a length (None, a generator) or the wrong number of results fails the batch with RuntimeError and the worker moves on; a CancelledError the handler raised itself cancels only that batch; and cancelling the worker cancels the batch in flight and everything still queued — no submit waits forever.

docs.title: Share loaded models
docs.text:
ModelRegistry keeps loaded models by id (LRU) — two call sites asking for the same model reuse the instance, and the least-recently-used one is unloaded (unload()) once over max_models:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import Embedder, ModelRegistry

registry = ModelRegistry(max_models=2)

def get_embedder(model_id: str) -> Embedder:
    return registry.get(model_id, lambda: Embedder(model_id))

A kept handle still counts toward max_models

Keeping the object get() returned (embedder = registry.get(...) at startup, used for every request) is safe with the SDK loaders. After an eviction, the next call on that handle does not reload behind the registry: it registers the model again under the same key (replacing any object a later get() built there), evicts the least-recently-used entry, and only then loads the weights. With max_models=1, keeping A, asking for B and using A again means three loads and two unloads, never both models resident at once.

When the evicted model still has calls running, whatever takes its place waits for them to finish before loading — both the readmitted handle and the new model from a get(). The exception is a call made from inside another model's call: it does not wait (the outer call may be exactly what the evicted model is waiting on), so there the ceiling is exceeded until the outer call ends. A third-party object that only implements unload() has no such hook — for those, call get() per request.

docs.title: What is loaded right now
docs.text:
