Process-local, volatile state

MemoryIdempotencyStore lives in process memory: each replica has its own dict and it is wiped on every restart / redeploy. Keys stored before a restart stop deduplicating afterwards. Use it only in dev / single-replica; for persistence across restarts and across replicas, use RedisIdempotencyStore.

docs.title: Production setup (multi-replica via Redis)
docs.text:
Installation

In-memory idempotency ships with tempest-fastapi-sdk — the minimum setup needs no extra. RedisIdempotencyStore needs the [cache] extra — uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[cache]" (pulls in redis).

from fastapi import FastAPI
from redis.asyncio import Redis
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    IdempotencyMiddleware,
    RedisIdempotencyStore,
)

from src.core.settings import settings


redis = Redis.from_url(settings.REDIS_URL)
app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(
    IdempotencyMiddleware,
    store=RedisIdempotencyStore(redis, prefix="idem:"),
    ttl_seconds=24 * 3600,
)

Why Redis.from_url here, not AsyncRedisManager?

This client feeds a middleware, built in create_app (sync), before any async lifespan runs. Redis.from_url() is lazy — it constructs without opening a connection, so it fits here. AsyncRedisManager needs await connect() and fits where there's an async context: a client via Depends(cache.client_dependency), or the SSEBroker built in the lifespan. Both need the [cache] extra (the redis package).

Stripe defaults to 24h — coherent with client-side exponential retry.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
import uuid
import httpx


async def create_charge(amount_cents: int) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Idempotent POST with automatic retry."""
    key = uuid.uuid4().hex
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as c:
        for _ in range(3):
            try:
                r = await c.post(
                    "https://api/charge",
                    json={"amount_cents": amount_cents},
                    headers={"Idempotency-Key": key},
                    timeout=10,
                )
                return r.json()
            except httpx.ReadTimeout:
                continue
        raise RuntimeError("3 retries failed")

Whichever of the 3 attempts reaches the server, the end state is the same resource created exactly once — remaining replicas receive the cached response.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Payments / charges
  • Webhook delivery (client retries with the same key)
  • External side-effect operations (email send, SMS)
  • Any POST /create whose retry could duplicate records

docs.title: When NOT to use
docs.text:
• GET (already idempotent)
  • Trivially reentrant operations (PATCH rewriting the same value)
  • When duplication has no consequence (logs, metrics)

docs.title: Custom backend
docs.text:
Implement the IdempotencyStore protocol:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import CachedResponse, IdempotencyStore


class DynamoIdempotencyStore:
    """Example DynamoDB-backed store."""

    async def get(self, key: str) -> CachedResponse | None:
        ...

    async def set(
        self,
        key: str,
        response: CachedResponse,
        *,
        ttl_seconds: int,
    ) -> None:
        ...


# Works with the middleware just like the built-in stores:
assert isinstance(DynamoIdempotencyStore(), IdempotencyStore)

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The Idempotency-Key header makes the server replay the same response on any retry once the first request completes — no duplicate record.
  • Only mutating verbs (POST / PUT / PATCH / DELETE) carrying the header are eligible; everything else passes straight through (opt-in per request).
  • There is an in-progress lock, per process: inside one replica, concurrent requests with the same key are serialized and the second replays the first's response. Across replicas it does not hold — keep client timeouts generous.
  • The key is scoped by credential (Authorization, Cookie, X-Token, X-API-Key); an anonymous request is not cached without allow_anonymous=True, and the same key with another request answers 422.
  • MemoryIdempotencyStore is process-local and volatile (dev / single-replica); RedisIdempotencyStore covers multi-replica and survives restarts.
  • Implement the IdempotencyStore protocol to plug in any backend (e.g. DynamoDB).

Next step: combine it with @cached to speed up reads, or with the Outbox pattern for reliable delivery of side-effects triggered by the handler.

docs.title: Image generation (local)
docs.text:
The SDK already generated text, understood images (VLM), embedded, transcribed and synthesized speech. What it could not do was draw. ImageGenerator closes that gap by running a HuggingFace diffusion model on your own hardware — no paid API, nothing leaving the machine.

uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[genai,genai-image]"

It mirrors TextGenerator

Same device/precision resolution, same lazy load, same unload_if_idle, same Hub pinning keywords (revision=/local_files_only=/trust_remote_code=). A service that already self-hosts an LLM gains images without learning a second set of conventions.

[genai-image] carries an upper bound

diffusers declares httpx<1.0.0 and huggingface-hub<2.0. Neither bites today (httpx is still on the 0.28 line), and being an optional extra the bound only enters the resolution of whoever installs it. Still: if your service comes to depend on httpx 1.x, this extra is the first place to look.

docs.title: The first drawing
docs.text:
import asyncio

from pathlib import Path

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerator

generator = ImageGenerator("stabilityai/sdxl-turbo")


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    images = await generator.generate("a lighthouse at dawn")
    Path("lighthouse.png").write_bytes(images[0].data)
    print(images[0].seed, images[0].width, images[0].height)


asyncio.run(main())

418223901 512 512

Notice what came back: not loose bytes, a list of GeneratedImage with the seed attached. Diffusion is deterministic given a seed, so returning it is the difference between "nice image, gone forever" and "nice image, and here is how to get it back". When you pass no seed, only the generator knows which one was drawn — which is why it reports it.

docs.title: Configuring: turbo and full models want opposite things
docs.text:
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerationConfig, ImageGenerator

turbo = ImageGenerator("stabilityai/sdxl-turbo")


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    images = await turbo.generate(
        "a lighthouse at dawn",
        config=ImageGenerationConfig(steps=4, guidance_scale=0.0, seed=7),
    )


asyncio.run(main())

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerationConfig, ImageGenerator

full = ImageGenerator("stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0")


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    images = await full.generate(
        "a lighthouse at dawn",
        config=ImageGenerationConfig(
            steps=30,
            guidance_scale=7.5,
            width=1024,
            height=1024,
            negative_prompt="blurry, watermark",
        ),
    )


asyncio.run(main())
Field Turbo / distilled model Full model steps 1–8 20–50 guidance_scale 0.0 5–9 width/height the model's native size 1024 on SDXL

Only what you set is sent

Unset fields fall through to the model's own defaults. That matters more here than for text: passing steps=30 to a turbo model wastes 26 of them, and passing guidance_scale=7.5 to it degrades the image.

docs.title: Reproducing
docs.text:
import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerationConfig, ImageGenerator

generator = ImageGenerator("stabilityai/sdxl-turbo")


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    first = await generator.generate(
        "a lighthouse at dawn",
        config=ImageGenerationConfig(seed=7, steps=4, guidance_scale=0.0),
    )
    again = await generator.generate(
        "a lighthouse at dawn",
        config=ImageGenerationConfig(seed=7, steps=4, guidance_scale=0.0),
    )
    print(first[0].data == again[0].data)


asyncio.run(main())

True

Same seed, same prompt, same hardware → same image. Across different GPUs the result can drift slightly (kernels and reduction order are not identical), so treat the seed as reproducibility on your host, not as a universal hash.

docs.title: Redrawing an existing image
docs.text:
import asyncio

from pathlib import Path

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerator

generator = ImageGenerator("stabilityai/sdxl-turbo")


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    edited = await generator.edit(
        "the same room, at night",
        "room.png",
        strength=0.6,
    )
    Path("room-night.png").write_bytes(edited[0].data)


asyncio.run(main())

strength says how far to move from the input: near 0.0 keeps the composition almost intact, 1.0 all but ignores the original. The input accepts a path, bytes, a PIL.Image or a NumPy array.

The edit pipeline costs no extra VRAM

It is built with AutoPipelineForImage2Image.from_pipe, which reuses the already-loaded UNet, VAE and text encoders instead of reading a second copy off disk. An SDXL pipeline is ~7 GB; loading it twice on one card is how a service OOMs at the first edit request.

docs.title: Serving it over HTTP
docs.text:
from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerator, make_genai_router

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(
    make_genai_router(image_generator=ImageGenerator("stabilityai/sdxl-turbo")),
)

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/genai/image \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt": "a lighthouse at dawn", "config": {"steps": 4, "guidance_scale": 0.0}}' \
  --output lighthouse.png --dump-header -

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: image/png
x-image-seed: 418223901

The response body is the image, so the route renders exactly one: a config.num_images above 1 gets 422 instead of rendering the batch and discarding the rest. The seed travels in the X-Image-Seed header. Want a batch? Use the class directly — the route exists for the common case of one image per request.

The route also answers 422 for a side above max_image_side (default 2048) and steps above max_image_steps (default 100), both from the GenAIRequestLimits that make_genai_router(limits=...) takes — see Per-request limits. ImageGenerationConfig itself already rejects width/height above 4096, steps above 500 and num_images above 16, on every path.

docs.title: Not holding the GPU hostage
docs.text:
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerator

generator = ImageGenerator(
    "stabilityai/sdxl-turbo",
    idle_unload_seconds=300.0,
)

A periodic task calls generator.unload_if_idle() and the VRAM comes back after five idle minutes. The next request reloads.

Concurrency defaults to 1, on purpose

Unlike an LLM, one diffusion call already saturates the GPU. Running two concurrently makes both slower and doubles peak VRAM. Raise max_concurrent only once you have measured spare card.

docs.title: Pinning the model, like everything else
docs.text:
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerator

generator = ImageGenerator(
    "stabilityai/sdxl-turbo",
    revision="f4b0486b498f84668e828044de1d0c8ba486e05b",
    cache_dir="/var/lib/models",
    local_files_only=True,
)

The same three keywords as every other loader. Download ahead of serving with tempest model pull and see Model weights (Hub lifecycle) — a diffusion pipeline is several gigabytes, and paying for it inside the first request hurts more here than anywhere else.

docs.title: Load-time decisions: pipeline_kwargs
docs.text:
Some choices happen while loading, not while drawing — and there the escape hatch is no help, because the cost is already paid. Pass those through pipeline_kwargs:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerator

generator = ImageGenerator(
    "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1",
    pipeline_kwargs={
        "safety_checker": None,
        "variant": "fp16",
        "use_safetensors": True,
    },
)
Key Why it matters safety_checker: None Stable Diffusion 1.x/2.x repositories bundle an extra CLIP purely to filter. It costs memory and sometimes returns a blank image. variant: "fp16" Fetches the half-precision weights — usually halves the download. use_safetensors: True Refuses a pickle checkpoint.

Turning the filter off is your call, and it has a licence

The Stable Diffusion licence asks that unfiltered results not be exposed publicly. Disable it knowing your use case — diffusers itself warns at runtime when you do.

Keys in pipeline_kwargs are applied last, so they win over whatever the SDK computed — that is also how you override torch_dtype.

docs.title: Swapping the scheduler (escape hatch)
docs.text:
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.genai import ImageGenerator

generator = ImageGenerator("stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0")
pipeline = generator.pipeline
print(type(pipeline).__name__)

.pipeline returns the diffusers object (loading it on first access). Use it to swap the scheduler, attach a LoRA or enable a memory optimization the SDK does not wrap — the SDK covers the common path and gets out of the way for the rest.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• generate(prompt, config=...) draws; it returns GeneratedImage carrying the seed that reproduces the result.
  • ImageGenerationConfig types steps/guidance_scale/width/ height/seed/num_images; turbo and full models want opposite values.
  • edit(prompt, image, strength=...) redraws, reusing the already-loaded components — no extra VRAM.
  • make_genai_router(image_generator=...) publishes POST /image, with the seed in the header.
  • idle_unload_seconds hands the VRAM back when nobody is drawing.
  • revision=/local_files_only= pin the model, exactly like the rest of the SDK.

Where to go next: Self-hosted generative AI for text, embeddings and RAG, and Model weights for the download lifecycle.

docs.title: Image metadata — cleaning a user's photo
docs.text:
A photo taken on a phone carries more than pixels. Inside the file go the GPS coordinates of where it was taken, the device make, model and sometimes serial number, the date and time, and now and then a thumbnail of the original photo, without the crop the user made.

Nobody sees any of this on screen. But when your service stores the photo, or forwards it to a third party (an AI provider, a partner, a public bucket), the metadata goes along. A profile picture becomes the home address of whoever sent it.

strip_image_metadata hands back the same image, in the same format, without any of that.

Required extra

uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[image]"
Brings only pillow. [all] already includes it.

docs.title: Your first clean upload route
docs.text:
A route that receives the photo, cleans it and writes it to disk:

# main.py

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Annotated
from uuid import uuid4

from fastapi import FastAPI, Form, UploadFile
from pydantic import BaseModel

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    ImageMediaTypeEnum,
    read_upload_capped,
    register_exception_handlers,
    strip_image_metadata,
)

MAX_PHOTO_BYTES: int = 10 * 1024 * 1024
PHOTOS_DIR: Path = Path("photos")


class PhotoResponseSchema(BaseModel):
    """Where the photo was stored, and how big it ended up."""

    key: str
    content_type: ImageMediaTypeEnum
    size: int


app = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)


@app.post("/photos")
async def upload_photo(
    content_type: Annotated[ImageMediaTypeEnum, Form()],
    file: UploadFile,
) -> PhotoResponseSchema:
    """Store the photo only after its metadata is gone."""
    data: bytes = await read_upload_capped(file, max_bytes=MAX_PHOTO_BYTES)
    clean: bytes = await asyncio.to_thread(strip_image_metadata, data, content_type)
    key: str = f"{uuid4()}.{content_type.extension}"
    PHOTOS_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    await asyncio.to_thread((PHOTOS_DIR / key).write_bytes, clean)
    return PhotoResponseSchema(key=key, content_type=content_type, size=len(clean))

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
This script builds a JPEG the way a phone saves one (GPS, device and an "upright" orientation), sends it to the route and checks the stored file:

# try_it.py

import io
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from PIL import Image
from PIL.ExifTags import GPS, IFD, Base

from main import PHOTOS_DIR, app


def phone_photo() -> bytes:
    """Build a JPEG the way a phone saves one: GPS, device and orientation."""
    exif = Image.Exif()
    exif[Base.Make] = "AcmePhone"
    exif[Base.Orientation] = 6
    exif[IFD.GPSInfo] = {GPS.GPSLatitudeRef: "S", GPS.GPSLatitude: (23.0, 33.0, 1.0)}
    buffer = io.BytesIO()
    Image.new("RGB", (400, 300), "teal").save(buffer, "JPEG", exif=exif)
    return buffer.getvalue()


def main() -> None:
    """Upload the photo and inspect what was stored."""
    client = TestClient(app)
    photo: bytes = phone_photo()
    response = client.post(
        "/photos",
        data={"content_type": "image/jpeg"},
        files={"file": ("photo.jpg", photo, "image/jpeg")},
    )
    print(response.status_code, response.json()["content_type"])
    stored: Path = PHOTOS_DIR / response.json()["key"]
    with Image.open(stored) as image:
        print("size:", image.size)
        print("exif tags:", len(image.getexif()))
    print("AcmePhone in the original:", b"AcmePhone" in photo)
    print("AcmePhone in the stored file:", b"AcmePhone" in stored.read_bytes())
    wrong = client.post(
        "/photos",
        data={"content_type": "image/png"},
        files={"file": ("photo.png", photo, "image/png")},
    )
    print(wrong.status_code, wrong.json()["code"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it with python try_it.py:

200 image/jpeg
size: (300, 400)
exif tags: 0
AcmePhone in the original: True
AcmePhone in the stored file: False
415 IMAGE_TYPE_MISMATCH

The uploaded photo was 400 x 300 with orientation tag 6 ("rotate 90° to display"). The stored one is 300 x 400 with no tag at all: the rotation was applied to the pixels before the EXIF went away, so it stays upright in any viewer. The same JPEG declared as PNG was refused.

docs.title: Read with a cap
docs.text: read_upload_capped stops reading at the byte cap, so a huge upload never lands in memory whole. That is the file limit; the pixel limit comes next.

docs.title: Clean off the event loop
docs.text:
strip_image_metadata decodes and encodes again: CPU work, in a synchronous function. Called directly in an async route, it blocks the event loop while it runs; asyncio.to_thread moves it to a thread and the server keeps serving.

Its second argument is the type the client declared. The function checks the bytes against it and refuses when they disagree: you never store a PNG with a .jpg extension.

docs.title: Store the result, never the original
docs.text:
After the cleaning, data should go nowhere. Store and forward only clean.

An error never hands the original bytes back

When the image does not decode, does not match the type or is over the ceiling, the function raises. There is no path where it returns data untouched "because it could not clean it", so a try/except that goes on storing the original would be an explicit choice by whoever wrote it, not an accident.

docs.title: What goes and what stays
docs.text:
Goes Stays EXIF (GPS, make, model, date, embedded thumbnail) the pixels, already in the right orientation XMP the size (width and height swapped when the orientation rotates by 90°) IPTC (the JPEG Photoshop 3.0 segment) the mode (RGB, RGBA, L, P...) ICC color profile the transparency comments (JPEG, GIF) and PNG text chunks (tEXt, iTXt, zTXt) the format

Accepted formats: JPEG, PNG, WEBP, GIF and BMP. The image/heic member of ImageMediaTypeEnum is refused with 415: Pillow ships no HEIC codec.

An animation becomes its first frame

Animated GIF and WEBP come back with only their first frame. Re-encoding every frame would multiply the cost by a frame count the client controls. If your service must keep animations, do not route that upload through here.

Without the ICC profile, color is read as sRGB

The color profile goes too, and the pixels are then read as sRGB. On a photo that was already sRGB nothing changes; on a wide-gamut photo (Display P3, common on recent phones) the color can shift slightly in saturation.

docs.title: The errors
docs.text:
They all extend AppException, so register_exception_handlers already turns them into a response with a code:

Exception Status code When ImageDecodeException 422 IMAGE_DECODE_FAILED the bytes are not an image of an accepted format, or are truncated ImageTypeMismatchException 415 IMAGE_TYPE_MISMATCH it is an image, but of a different format than declared ImageFormatUnsupportedException 415 IMAGE_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED the declared type is not one the function re-encodes (image/heic, application/pdf) ImageTooLargeException 413 IMAGE_TOO_LARGE the image has more pixels than max_pixels

ImageTypeMismatchException and ImageFormatUnsupportedException extend InvalidFileTypeException, and ImageTooLargeException extends FileTooLargeException: an except that already caught those two keeps catching.

docs.title: The pixel ceiling
docs.text:
A PNG of a few KB can declare 20 000 x 20 000 pixels. Decoded, it turns into gigabytes of memory: a decompression bomb. That is why the function reads width and height from the header and checks them against max_pixels before decoding any pixel:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import DEFAULT_MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, strip_image_metadata


def clean_avatar(data: bytes) -> bytes:
    """Clean an avatar, accepting at most 4 000 x 4 000 pixels."""
    return strip_image_metadata(data, "image/jpeg", max_pixels=16_000_000)


print(DEFAULT_MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS)

The default is DEFAULT_MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (50 million), which fits the full photo of a 48 or 50 MP sensor. Memory grows with the pixels: measured on Pillow 13.0.0 with an 8000 x 6000 JPEG, the call's peak rose by about 186 MB for an upright photo and 368 MB for one its orientation rotates by 90°. Raise the ceiling with that in mind.

Technical details: Pillow's global ceiling

Pillow has its own guard, PIL.Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (about 89.5 million by default), which applies to the whole process. The function does not touch it. It still runs when the file is opened: above it Pillow emits a DecompressionBombWarning, and above twice that it refuses on its own. Both cases reach you as ImageTooLargeException (the warning when you escalate it to an error; otherwise the function's ceiling refuses right after).

docs.title: Re-encoding quality
docs.text:
Format How it comes back JPEG jpeg_quality, default DEFAULT_JPEG_QUALITY (90; Pillow's is 75) Lossless WEBP stays lossless Lossy WEBP webp_quality, default DEFAULT_WEBP_QUALITY (90) PNG, GIF, BMP lossless, as always

JPEG is re-encoded lossy, so the bytes change even for a photo that had no metadata at all. The function does not resize.

Technical details: why re-encode instead of cutting segments

You can drop a JPEG's EXIF by cutting its APP1 segment. But each format hides metadata somewhere else: APP1 (EXIF and XMP) and APP13 (IPTC) in JPEG, eXIf, iCCP, tEXt, iTXt and zTXt in PNG, EXIF, XMP and ICCP in WEBP, comment extensions in GIF. A hand-written cutter misses the case it does not know. The function opens the image through Pillow's decoder, keeps only the pixels (and the transparency they need) and encodes again without passing exif=, icc_profile= or pnginfo=, so whatever the source file carried has no way back.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• strip_image_metadata(data, content_type) returns the image in the same format, without EXIF, XMP, IPTC, ICC, comments and text chunks.
  • The EXIF orientation is applied to the pixels before it goes: the photo stays upright.
  • A declared type that differs from the real one, bytes that do not decode and an image above max_pixels raise a typed error; the original never comes back.
  • In an async route, call it through asyncio.to_thread.
  • An animation comes back as its first frame; HEIC is refused.
  • Extra [image] (only pillow).

See also: Uploads, to receive and validate the file before cleaning it.

docs.title: Introspection auth (resource server)
docs.text:
Not every service issues its own tokens. Often your service is just a resource server in the OAuth2 pattern: it receives an opaque bearer minted by an upstream identity provider and must validate it by asking that provider who owns the token. You don't decode a JWT or verify a signature — you call a userinfo / introspection endpoint and trust the response.

IntrospectionAuth wraps exactly that pattern:

  • it validates the bearer by calling GET <userinfo_url> with Authorization: Bearer <token>,
  • it caches successful lookups in-process for a short TTL, so a burst of requests carrying the same token doesn't hammer the upstream,
  • with audiences=, it binds the token to this service: the response must name one of them in aud, azp or client_id,
  • it can optionally gate access on an application claim (access_apps by default), and
  • it extracts the user id from the subject claim (sub by default).

Installation

IntrospectionAuth needs the [http] extra — uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[http]" (pulls in httpx, used to call the upstream userinfo).

When to use this

Use it when another service (IAGRO, a Keycloak, an Auth0, your own identity service) mints the tokens and your service only needs to accept them. If your service is the one that logs users in and issues tokens, you want UserAuthService + make_auth_router (see Auth flow), not this.

docs.title: The minimal path
docs.text:
Instantiate once, pointing at the provider's userinfo endpoint, and use the two methods as FastAPI dependencies:

# src/api/dependencies/auth.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth

from src.core.settings import settings

auth = IntrospectionAuth(
    userinfo_url=settings.IAGRO_USERINFO_URL,   # e.g. https://id.iagro.gov/users/me
    audiences=["famacha-api"],                  # this service's client id at the provider
    required_app="famacha",                     # per-app access gate
)

# src/api/routers/animals.py

from typing import Any
from uuid import UUID

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends

from src.api.dependencies.auth import auth
from src.services.animals import animals


router = APIRouter(prefix="/api/animals", tags=["animals"])


@router.get("/me")
async def whoami(
    claims: dict[str, Any] = Depends(auth.get_claims),
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Return the raw claims of the authenticated user."""
    return claims


@router.get("/")
async def list_animals(
    user_id: UUID = Depends(auth.get_user_id),
) -> list[str]:
    """List the user's animals — id already resolved from the token."""
    return await animals.list_for(user_id)

animals is your application's glue

animals.list_for(...) stands in for your own service/repository layer — it is not part of the SDK. Swap it for your project's real call.

That's it. A request without Authorization gets 401; a token the upstream rejects gets 401; a token issued to another client of the provider gets 401; a user without famacha in access_apps gets 403.

Wire up the exception handlers

IntrospectionAuth raises the SDK's own UnauthorizedException (401) and ForbiddenException (403). Call register_exception_handlers(app) (the create_app() that tempest new generates already does) so they become the right HTTP statuses instead of 500.

docs.title: How it works, piece by piece
get_claims — the heart
docs.text:
get_claims is the primary dependency. It:

  1. reads the bearer via HTTPBearer(auto_error=False) — no header → UnauthorizedException;
  2. calls fetch_userinfo(token) (cached), which with audiences refuses the response for a token issued to another client;
  3. if required_app is set, requires it to be in claims.get(app_claim) or [], otherwise ForbiddenException;
  4. returns the claims dict.
import asyncio
from typing import Any

from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth

from src.core.settings import settings

auth = IntrospectionAuth(userinfo_url=settings.IAGRO_USERINFO_URL)

credentials = HTTPAuthorizationCredentials(
    scheme="Bearer",
    credentials="eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.token",
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    claims: dict[str, Any] = await auth.get_claims(credentials)
    # {"sub": "…", "access_apps": ["famacha"], "email": "…", ...}


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: get_user_id — the common shortcut
docs.text:
Most routes only want the user id, not the whole dict. get_user_id depends on the same bearer, calls get_claims internally, and does UUID(str(claims["sub"])):

import asyncio
from uuid import UUID

from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth

from src.core.settings import settings

auth = IntrospectionAuth(userinfo_url=settings.IAGRO_USERINFO_URL)

credentials = HTTPAuthorizationCredentials(
    scheme="Bearer",
    credentials="eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.token",
)


async def main() -> None:
    """Run this example."""
    user_id: UUID = await auth.get_user_id(credentials)


asyncio.run(main())

A missing subject, or one that isn't a valid UUID, becomes UnauthorizedException.

Why doesn't get_user_id declare Depends(self.get_claims)?

Default arguments are evaluated at method-definition time, when the self instance doesn't exist yet — so you can't write Depends(self.get_claims) in the signature. The fix: get_user_id depends on the bearer directly and calls await self.get_claims(credentials) in its body. It still wires cleanly as Depends(auth.get_user_id).

docs.title: Bind the token to this service — audiences
docs.text:
A 200 from userinfo proves the token is valid at the provider, not that it was issued to your service. A provider that serves several clients (your app, a partner app, an internal tool) usually answers userinfo for the token of any of them. Without a binding, a token the user handed to another app at the same provider authenticates here as that user — and whoever runs that app can replay it.

audiences= closes that: the response must name one of the values in aud (a string or a list), azp or client_id. None of them matches, or the response carries none of the three → 401, and the refused response is not cached.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth

auth = IntrospectionAuth(
    userinfo_url="https://id.example.com/users/me",
    audiences=["famacha-api"],
)
Upstream response With audiences=["famacha-api"] {"sub": "…", "aud": "famacha-api"} accepted {"sub": "…", "aud": ["account", "famacha-api"]} accepted {"sub": "…", "aud": "account", "azp": "famacha-api"} accepted (Keycloak) {"sub": "…", "client_id": "famacha-api"} accepted (RFC 7662) {"sub": "…", "aud": "other-app", "azp": "other-app"} 401 {"sub": "…"} 401

Without audiences, behaviour is unchanged — with a warning

The parameter is optional so existing users of the class keep working, but an instance built without it logs a WARNING on the tempest_fastapi_sdk.auth.introspection logger, once per instance. If your provider returns none of these claims from userinfo, check whether it exposes introspection (RFC 7662), which returns client_id.

docs.title: The cache
docs.text:
Every 200 response is stored for cache_ttl_seconds (30 by default), with a time.monotonic() clock and the raw token as the key. Within the TTL, the second call does not hit the upstream. A 401/403 evicts the token immediately. cache_ttl_seconds=0 disables caching.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth

from src.core.settings import settings


auth = IntrospectionAuth(
    userinfo_url=settings.IAGRO_USERINFO_URL,
    cache_ttl_seconds=60,   # tolerate up to 60s of a revoked token
)

TTL is a revocation window

While a claim is cached, an upstream revocation isn't seen. Pick a short TTL (seconds to a few minutes) to balance provider load against freshness. 0 disables the cache and always revalidates.

docs.title: Lazy URL (callable)
docs.text:
userinfo_url accepts a str or a zero-argument callable, resolved on every call. That lets you pass a settings property read only at runtime (handy when the URL arrives late from the environment, or varies per tenant):

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth

from src.core.settings import settings


auth = IntrospectionAuth(
    userinfo_url=lambda: settings.IAGRO_USERINFO_URL,
)

docs.title: Custom claims
docs.text:
If your provider uses different names, tweak them:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth

from src.core.settings import settings


auth = IntrospectionAuth(
    userinfo_url=settings.IDP_USERINFO_URL,
    required_app="famacha",
    app_claim="apps",        # instead of "access_apps"
    subject_claim="user_id", # instead of "sub"
)

docs.title: HTTP client
docs.text:
By default the instance creates one shared httpx.AsyncClient (lazily, with httpx.Timeout(timeout)) and reuses it. You can inject your own — handy in tests or to share a pool / limits:

import httpx

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth

from src.core.settings import settings


client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=httpx.Timeout(5.0))
auth = IntrospectionAuth(
    userinfo_url=settings.IDP_USERINFO_URL,
    http_client=client,
)

The cache is per instance, not global — the app can create several IntrospectionAuth objects (one per upstream) without one leaking state into another.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Inject an httpx.AsyncClient with a MockTransport so you never touch the network:

import httpx
import pytest
from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import IntrospectionAuth


def _handler(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
    assert request.headers["Authorization"] == "Bearer tok"
    return httpx.Response(200, json={"sub": "…", "access_apps": ["famacha"]})


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_valid_token() -> None:
    auth = IntrospectionAuth(
        userinfo_url="https://id.example.com/users/me",
        required_app="famacha",
        http_client=httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.MockTransport(_handler)),
    )
    creds = HTTPAuthorizationCredentials(scheme="Bearer", credentials="tok")
    claims = await auth.get_claims(creds)
    assert claims["access_apps"] == ["famacha"]

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• IntrospectionAuth is for the resource server pattern: it validates opaque bearers against an upstream userinfo — it never issues tokens.
  • get_claims and get_user_id are bound methods usable directly as Depends(auth.get_claims) / Depends(auth.get_user_id).
  • No credentials → 401; rejected token / upstream down → 401; token of another client (with audiences) → 401; app not granted → 403; invalid subject → 401.
  • Pass audiences= with the service's client id: without it, a token issued to another app at the same provider authenticates here.
  • In-process per-token cache with a time.monotonic() TTL; 401/403 evicts; cache_ttl_seconds=0 disables it.
  • userinfo_url can be a str or a callable (resolved per call); claims (app_claim, subject_claim) and the httpx client are configurable. Cache and client are per instance.

docs.title: Jobs — long work with a status
docs.text:
A queue hands the call to a worker. It answers none of what the person in front of the screen is asking:

  • has anything picked this up, or is it still queued?
  • is it running right now?
  • did it finish? what did it produce?
  • if it stopped, why — in their language, not as a traceback.

TaskIQ's AsyncResultBackend comes close, but it is keyed by task id, holds the function's return value, and is not a table the application queries, paginates or shows in an admin. What the interface wants is a row.

This is the symmetric half of the outbox: there it is a message to publish, here it is work to execute.

docs.title: 1. The table
docs.text:
Subclass BaseJobModel and pick a __tablename__ — exactly like BaseOutboxModel:

# src/db/models/job.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import BaseJobModel


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """One unit of long-running work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"

Three lines, because the rest comes with it: kind, status, params, payload, result_id, error, attempts, max_attempts, started_at, finished_at — plus the id / is_active / created_at / updated_at every BaseModel has.

Column What for kind which work this is; the worker branches on it and the interface filters by it status queued → running → done / failed, indexed params small input, as JSON payload large input — the file a broker should not be carrying result_id the row the work produced, so the screen links straight to it error why it stopped, written for the user

docs.title: 2. Enqueue
docs.text:
JobStore takes the AsyncDatabaseManager, not a session: every call opens and closes its own, because its users are a handler that enqueues, a worker that grinds for minutes, and a screen asking every couple of seconds — none of them should hold a session across that.

# src/api/routers/extraction.py
from uuid import UUID

from fastapi import APIRouter, UploadFile

from src.db.models.job import JobModel
from src.api.dependencies.resources import db
from src.tasks import extract_document

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import JobStore

router = APIRouter(prefix="/api/extraction")
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel, stale_after=300.0)


@router.post("/")
async def start_extraction(file: UploadFile) -> dict[str, UUID]:
    """Accept the document and return the job id to follow."""
    job = await store.enqueue(
        "extract",
        params={"filename": file.filename or "unnamed.pdf"},
        payload=await file.read(),
    )
    await extract_document.enqueue(str(job.id))
    return {"job_id": job.id}

That order is deliberate: write the row, then send the task. The row is what the interface reads, and it has to exist before the worker can claim it.

docs.title: 3. The worker
docs.text:
# src/tasks/__init__.py
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import BaseJobModel, JobStore, TaskQueue


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """One unit of long-running work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"


class UnsupportedFormat(Exception):
    """The uploaded file is not something we know how to read."""


async def read_tender(payload: bytes | None) -> UUID:
    """The real work; returns the id of what it produced.

    Args:
        payload (bytes | None): The document claimed with the job.

    Returns:
        UUID: The id of the generated draft.

    Raises:
        UnsupportedFormat: When the document cannot be read.
    """
    if not payload:
        raise UnsupportedFormat("empty file")
    return uuid4()


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
tq = TaskQueue.rabbitmq("amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/", resources=[db])
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel, stale_after=300.0)


@tq.task
async def extract_document(job_id: str) -> None:
    """Claim the job, do the work, close the row.

    Args:
        job_id (str): The id the route sent along with the task.
    """
    job = await store.claim(UUID(job_id))
    if job is None:
        return
    try:
        draft_id = await read_tender(job.payload)
    except UnsupportedFormat as exc:
        await store.fail(job.id, f"I could not read the file: {exc}")
    else:
        await store.succeed(job.id, result_id=draft_id)

Three things happening there, each for a reason:

  • claim is what separates "queued" from "running". Without it the interface cannot tell "the worker is busy" from "nobody picked it up" — which is the exact question when something takes a while.
  • claim returns None when the job is not yours (someone else claimed it, or the id does not exist). It is a conditional UPDATE, so two workers racing for one id cannot both win: one sees a row change, the other does not.
  • succeed / fail drop the payload. Without that, the table of finished jobs becomes a pile of documents.

Do not hold the session across the work

claim already returned the payload; from there the worker works with no session open and only comes back to close the row. A transaction that reads first and writes minutes later is the case no busy_timeout can rescue — see Database.

docs.title: A column of your own, written with done
docs.text:
A job that generates a file has to record where the file went. That column belongs to your model, not to the SDK — and it has to reach the row in the same UPDATE that marks it done:

# src/tasks/export.py
from uuid import UUID

from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import BaseJobModel, JobStore, TaskQueue


class ExportJobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """An export that produces a file for the user to download."""

    __tablename__ = "export_jobs"

    object_key: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(255), nullable=True)


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
tq = TaskQueue.rabbitmq("amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/", resources=[db])
store: JobStore[ExportJobModel] = JobStore(db, model=ExportJobModel)


async def build_archive(job_id: UUID) -> str:
    """Generate the file and return its storage key.

    Args:
        job_id (UUID): The job that asked for the file.

    Returns:
        str: The key of the stored object.
    """
    return f"exports/{job_id}.zip"


@tq.task
async def export_data(job_id: str) -> None:
    """Generate the file and close the job pointing at it.

    Args:
        job_id (str): The id the route sent along with the task.
    """
    job = await store.claim(UUID(job_id))
    if job is None:
        return
    key = await build_archive(job.id)
    await store.succeed(job.id, values={"object_key": key})

Why not write object_key from a session of your own and then call succeed? Because that is two transactions, and between them the row is running with the key already set. A cancel landing in that window makes succeed raise JobCancelledError — and leaves a cancelled row pointing at a file the worker is about to delete. With values the key goes into the same conditional UPDATE as done: a cancelled job gets nothing.

values only takes your own columns

A name that is not a column of the model, or one the store controls (status, finished_at, result_id, progress, ... — the full list is STORE_OWNED_JOB_COLUMNS), raises ValueError before any SQL runs. result_id has its own parameter; the rest are the transition succeed exists to make.

docs.title: 4. The screen asking "is it done yet?"
docs.text:
# src/ui/pages/extraction.py
from uuid import UUID

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import BaseJobModel, JobStore


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """One unit of long-running work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel)


async def show_progress(job_id: UUID) -> list[str]:
    """Follow the job until it finishes.

    Args:
        job_id (UUID): The job the screen is watching.

    Returns:
        list[str]: Every status the job went through.
    """
    seen: list[str] = []
    async for job in store.watch(job_id, interval=2.0):
        seen.append(job.status)
    return seen

watch yields the job on every status change, until a terminal state, and then ends. The current status comes out immediately, so a caller subscribing after the job already finished still gets exactly one value.

The detail this helper exists to stop you getting wrong: no session is held between ticks. Each poll opens and closes its own, so the worker writing to the same database is never blocked by the screen watching it.

timeout= gives up with TimeoutError instead of waiting forever.

docs.title: 5. The worker that died holding the job
docs.text:
A running row nobody will ever close is the failure a queue cannot see: the task is gone, the row is not. reclaim_stale() readmits it:

# src/tasks/__init__.py
from uuid import UUID

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import BaseJobModel, JobStore, TaskQueue


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """One unit of long-running work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
tq = TaskQueue.rabbitmq("amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/", resources=[db])
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel, stale_after=300.0)


@tq.task
async def extract_document(job_id: str) -> None:
    """Claim the job and close the row.

    Args:
        job_id (str): The id the route sent along with the task.
    """
    job = await store.claim(UUID(job_id))
    if job is None:
        return
    await store.succeed(job.id)


@tq.interval(seconds=60)
async def reclaim_jobs() -> None:
    """Requeue what a dead worker left in RUNNING, and send it again."""
    reclaimed = await store.reclaim_stale()
    for job_id in reclaimed.requeued:
        await extract_document.enqueue(str(job_id))


async def send_job(job: JobModel) -> None:
    """Hand one job to the worker.

    Args:
        job (JobModel): The row going to the queue.
    """
    await extract_document.enqueue(str(job.id))


@tq.interval(seconds=300)
async def redispatch_jobs() -> None:
    """Resend `queued` rows whose send was lost."""
    await store.redispatch_queued(send_job, older_than=600.0)

Rows whose started_at is older than stale_after go back to queued — unless they already spent their max_attempts, in which case they are closed as failed. Without that budget, a job that kills its worker would be readmitted forever.

Going back to queued is not enough. That job's message died with the worker, and nothing in the SDK sends a queued row to the queue on its own — which is why reclaim_stale() returns the ids (ReclaimedJobs.requeued and ReclaimedJobs.failed), and reclaim_jobs above resends them straight away.

redispatch_queued covers the other way a row stays queued forever: the row's enqueue succeeded and the task's send did not (broker down, process died between the two steps). It resends queued rows nobody touched for more than older_than (age is updated_at, which it refreshes on every send — so each row goes out at most once per window).

Sending twice is harmless

A row whose message is merely waiting in a long backlog is resent too. Both messages reach claim, and its conditional UPDATE lets exactly one of them run; the other gets None and returns. Pick an older_than above the backlog you expect so this stays rare — not to keep it correct.

reclaim_stale() no longer returns an int

It used to return the count; it now returns ReclaimedJobs. len() and truthiness still work (if await store.reclaim_stale():), but == 1 or adding to a number does not: use .total.

Without stale_after, the method refuses

JobStore(db, model=JobModel) with no stale_after raises RuntimeError from reclaim_stale() rather than guessing a threshold.

docs.title: 6. Listing
docs.text:
# src/services/extraction.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import BaseJobModel, JobStatusEnum, JobStore


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """One unit of long-running work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel)


async def dashboard() -> tuple[list[JobModel], list[JobModel]]:
    """Read what the progress screen shows.

    Returns:
        tuple[list[JobModel], list[JobModel]]: The recent jobs and the
        ones running right now.
    """
    recent = await store.list_recent(kind="extract", limit=20)
    running = await store.list_recent(status=JobStatusEnum.RUNNING)
    return recent, running

Returns [] when nothing matches — "no jobs yet" is a successful answer, not a 404.

docs.title: 7. Cancelling
docs.text:
The user clicked "cancel". Nothing in TaskIQ — or in any broker the SDK speaks — offers "kill the task with this id": once it is running inside the worker process, only that process can stop it. So cancellation is cooperative: the request writes cancelled and answers immediately; the worker reads that status at agreed checkpoints and gives up.

# src/services/extraction.py
from uuid import UUID

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import BaseJobModel, JobStore


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """A unit of long-running work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel)


async def cancel(job_id: UUID) -> bool:
    """Ask the job to stop.

    Args:
        job_id (UUID): The job to cancel.

    Returns:
        bool: True when there was something to stop.
    """
    job: JobModel | None = await store.cancel(job_id, reason="cancelled by the user")
    return job is not None

Idempotent on purpose

cancel() returns None — rather than raising — when there is nothing to stop: an unknown id, a job already done, already failed, or already cancelled. Double-clicking, or clicking just as the job finished on its own, is not an error.

docs.title: The worker gives up
docs.text:
run_cancellable is the checkpoint that runs during the work rather than between steps. It races the coroutine against a predicate polled on an interval, and when the predicate says stop, the coroutine is cancelled for real — an in-flight HTTP request is aborted and the worker is free within the poll interval, instead of finishing a call whose result nobody wants.

# src/tasks/extract.py
from uuid import UUID

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import (
    BaseJobModel,
    JobStore,
    StageInterruptedError,
    run_cancellable,
)


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """A unit of long-running work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel)


async def summarize(text: str) -> str:
    """Genuinely long work (a network call, cancellable).

    Args:
        text (str): The text to summarize.

    Returns:
        str: The summary.
    """
    return text[:100]


async def run(job_id: UUID) -> None:
    """Run the job, giving up if it is cancelled midway.

    Args:
        job_id (UUID): The job to run.
    """
    job: JobModel | None = await store.claim(job_id)
    if job is None:
        return

    try:
        summary: str = await run_cancellable(
            summarize("a long text"),
            interrupted=store.cancellation_watch(job_id),
        )
    except StageInterruptedError:
        return

    await store.succeed(job_id)
    print(summary)

Only works on genuinely cancellable awaits

Work handed to asyncio.to_thread is not cancellable: cancelling the coroutine abandons the wrapper while the thread runs on to completion, still holding the CPU and still competing with the next job. For that shape — local inference, say — check between steps, and check again before writing the result.

succeed refuses to land on top of a cancellation

A worker that raced past its last checkpoint still cannot overwrite the row: succeed()/fail() raise JobCancelledError, a subclass of JobAlreadyFinishedError. The two are distinct on purpose — a plain JobAlreadyFinishedError says two workers believe the job is theirs, while this one says the system did exactly what it was told. Log it and move on; do not alert.

cancelled is terminal, but it is not a failure

It joins TERMINAL_JOB_STATUSES (the poll stops, the payload is dropped), but nothing went wrong. An interface that highlights failed should leave this one alone, and an alert that pages on failures should not fire.

docs.title: 8. Progress: the bar that does not lie
docs.text:
A status answers "is it done yet?". It does not answer "how much longer?" — and that is the question of whoever has been watching the screen for a minute and a half.

There are two dishonest ways to answer. A bar that crawls on a timer tells a story unrelated to the work. A bar that jumps 0 to 100 when the work ends is a spinner wearing a percentage.

The third way is to measure. Run the real work over real inputs, take the median of each phase, and declare what you measured:

# src/tasks/plan.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import PhasePlan

PLAN: PhasePlan = PhasePlan.from_seconds(
    {"pdf": 1.0, "table": 30.0, "reading": 19.0},
    per_kilochar={"table": 0.5, "reading": 0.2},
)

The medians are the weights: a phase that takes half the time takes half the bar. per_kilochar is the slope fitted against input size — with it, a call over 40,000 characters is not paced like one over 4,000.

The worker then runs each phase through the ProgressTracker:

# src/tasks/extract.py
from uuid import UUID

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import (
    BaseJobModel,
    JobStore,
    PhasePlan,
    ProgressTracker,
    StageInterruptedError,
)


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """One unit of long work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel)
PLAN: PhasePlan = PhasePlan.from_seconds({"table": 30.0, "reading": 19.0})


async def read_table(text: str) -> str:
    """Call the model to transcribe the table.

    Args:
        text (str): The pages carrying the table.

    Returns:
        str: The model's reply.
    """
    return text


async def read_document(job_id: UUID, text: str) -> None:
    """Read a document, reporting the progress of each phase.

    Args:
        job_id (UUID): The claimed job.
        text (str): The already-extracted document.
    """
    tracker = ProgressTracker(store, job_id, plan=PLAN)
    try:
        table = await tracker.run("table", read_table(text), size=len(text))
    except StageInterruptedError:
        return
    await store.succeed(job_id, result_id=None)
    del table

Every tick writes progress and stage on the row, and a phase never fills: the interpolation stops at 95% of its span, because "the table call is done" is something only the table call finishing can say.

One poll answers both questions

The tick that writes progress is the one that asks whether the user cancelled — same row, same interval. Asking twice would double the traffic to say the same thing.

A real count beats the interpolation

When the phase can count — pages extracted out of pages total — use await tracker.report("pdf", done=read / total). A measured number beats an estimate, and only it may reach the phase ceiling.

Your own work in a thread

Cancelling the coroutine does not stop a thread. A TextGenerator already handles its own case: when tracker.run cancels the call, it sets the event the model checks after every token. For your work running in a thread, pass a threading.Event to tracker.run(..., stop_event=event) and check it in your loop. Without it, the screen says "cancelled" while the thread keeps working.

On the screen side, ask watch to emit on progress changes too, or the bar will not move:

# src/ui/pages/extraction.py
from uuid import UUID

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.db import AsyncDatabaseManager
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import BaseJobModel, JobStatusEnum, JobStore


class JobModel(BaseJobModel):
    """One unit of long work in this application."""

    __tablename__ = "jobs"


db = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./app.db")
store: JobStore[JobModel] = JobStore(db, model=JobModel)


async def follow(job_id: UUID) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Follow a reading to the end, frame by frame.

    Args:
        job_id (UUID): The job to follow.

    Returns:
        list[tuple[str, float]]: Each phase and the percentage at that moment.
    """
    frames: list[tuple[str, float]] = []
    async for job in store.watch(
        job_id,
        interval=2.0,
        emit_on=("status", "progress", "stage"),
    ):
        frames.append((job.stage, job.progress))
    return frames


async def in_flight() -> list[JobModel]:
    """List what the progress strip shows.

    Returns:
        list[JobModel]: The queued jobs and the running ones.
    """
    return await store.list_recent(
        kind="extract",
        statuses=(JobStatusEnum.QUEUED, JobStatusEnum.RUNNING),
    )

Plural statuses is what a progress screen actually asks: "queued or running" is one question, and asking it as two queries makes the two halves disagree the moment a worker claims a job between them.

docs.title: 9. Several stages on the record itself
docs.text:
JobStore above gives long work its own row. That is right when the work is the thing — an export, an import, a batch. It is the wrong shape when the work decorates a record the interface is already showing: a document that gets transcribed, then summarized, then mined for suggestions. There the screen already fetches the document, and a second table means a second query and a join to render one page.

The alternative is status columns on the record — summary_status, summary_error, one triple per stage. That works, and it rots in a specific way: each stage grows its own copy of "set running" and "mark failed", a fix has to land N times, and a copy-pasted stage that kept a neighbour's column name compiles, imports, and reports the neighbour's state.

StageMap is that table written once.

# src/core/stages.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import StageMap, StageStatusEnum

STAGES: StageMap = StageMap(
    ["transcription", "summary", "suggestions"],
    prefix="doc_",
)

That resolves doc_status_summary, doc_error_summary and doc_result_summary. The templates are configurable, because column naming is a house convention rather than something a library imposes.

# src/tasks/summarize.py
from typing import Any

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.tasks import StageMap, StageStatusEnum

STAGES: StageMap = StageMap(["summary"], prefix="doc_")


async def summarize(text: str) -> str:
    """Long work.

    Args:
        text (str): The text to summarize.

    Returns:
        str: The summary.
    """
    return text[:100]


async def run(document: Any) -> None:
    """Run the stage, writing only if it is still ours.

    Args:
        document (Any): The record, freshly read from the database.
    """
    STAGES.mark(document, "summary", StageStatusEnum.RUNNING)
    summary: str = await summarize("a long text")

    if STAGES.owns(document, "summary", StageStatusEnum.RUNNING):
        STAGES.mark(document, "summary", StageStatusEnum.DONE, result=summary)

owns is an ownership check, not a cancellation check

"This stage is no longer mine" covers two things: the user cancelled, and a newer run restarted the stage. In both cases the old run must not write — one would resurrect work that was stopped, the other would clobber a fresher result.

Re-read the record from the database before calling it. An object loaded before the work started still holds the old status and would answer True no matter what happened meanwhile.

Cancelling is deliberately partial

STAGES.cancel(document) returns (cancelled, ignored). A stage that already finished lands in ignored rather than raising: a screen polling for status will routinely ask to cancel something that completed a moment ago.

There is no cascade, and none is needed: if each stage only enqueues the next on success, cancelling the first means the second never exists.

Marking without a result does not erase the previous one

Cancelling a regeneration keeps the old summary — it is still the best answer available. Wiping it would make cancelling strictly worse than never asking.

The map declares no columns

The mapped_column declarations are yours. Migrations, types and indexes stay where a reader expects them; the map only agrees with you on the naming. It refuses at construction when two stages would resolve to the same column — the copy-paste bug nothing else in the stack would notice.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Exception When JobNotFoundError the id does not exist (get, succeed, fail, watch) JobAlreadyFinishedError closing a job that is already terminal — two workers believe it is theirs JobCancelledError closing a job the user cancelled midway; a subclass of the above, so a worker can tell "we did as told" from "the concurrency is wrong" StageInterruptedError run_cancellable saw the cancellation; not a failure, the handler just returns

They are LookupError / RuntimeError, not AppException: the store runs in the worker as often as in a request, and a worker has no HTTP status to answer with. Translate at the boundary with not_found_exception(...).

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The queue hands the call to a worker; it answers none of what the person in front of the screen is asking. JobStore gives long work a row of its own, and that row is what the screen reads.
  • BaseJobModel is abstract: your service ships the concrete table and picks the __tablename__.
  • JobStore takes the AsyncDatabaseManager, not a session — each operation opens and closes its own, because a worker and a request do not share a unit of work.
  • reclaim_stale exists because a running row nobody will ever close is the failure the queue cannot see: the process died holding the job. It returns the ids, because a queued row with no message never runs; redispatch_queued resends what stayed queued without a send.
  • succeed(values=...) writes your model's column in the same UPDATE as done — a cancelled job gets nothing.
  • Cancelling is cooperative: the request writes CANCELLED and the worker aborts at its next checkpoint. No broker kills in-flight work for you.
  • Status answers "is it done?"; progress answers "how much is left?". Those are different questions: PhasePlan + ProgressTracker turn a measured phase into the percentage the row carries, and watch(emit_on=...) is what makes the bar move between two status changes. StageMap covers the third question — several stages on one record.
  • The store raises LookupError / RuntimeError, not AppException: it runs in the worker, where there is no request to turn into an HTTP response.

docs.title: Kestra (workflow orchestrator)
docs.text:
Kestra runs declarative YAML flows — call an API, wait, retry, chain steps. Your service talks to it in two directions, and both already fit the SDK's building blocks:

  • Service → Kestra: the service triggers a flow (webhook or execution API) with the HTTPClient.
  • Kestra → service: the flow calls a service route through the io.kestra.plugin.core.http.Request task, protected by make_token_dependency.

And since triggering a flow from a database write is the classic dual write, the finish is the outbox (delivery to Kestra) + WebhookInbox (receives the result exactly once) pair.

No new SDK module, on purpose

The whole contract is "POST with a header" in both directions, and HTTPClient already brings retry, circuit breaker and default_headers. A KestraClient would only pay off if two services copied the same call. There is no new dependency either: not even Kestra's Python SDK, which would be an HTTP wrapper carrying its version bounds into your lock.

Everything here was executed

Every command and every output on this page came from a real run against Kestra 2.0.6 OSS (kestra/kestra:v2.0.6-slim, digest sha256:82f7c84f00fb883a6ff93c6d07e31f30eaabd0c84d229fb56a80edeeecd8dbba) with a local FastAPI service, Python 3.12. Another Kestra version may answer differently — the tenant section exists because of that.

docs.title: 1. Start Kestra for testing
docs.text:
docker run -d --name lab-kestra -p 18080:8080 \
  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  -e SECRET_SERVICE_TOKEN=dG9vbC1zZWNyZXQtMTIz \
  -e SECRET_WEBHOOK_KEY=aG9vay1rZXktYWJjMTIz \
  -e KESTRA_CONFIGURATION='
kestra:
  server:
    basic-auth:
      username: admin@example.com
      password: Kestra12345!
' \
  kestra/kestra:v2.0.6-slim server local

What each piece does:

  • --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway lets the flow (inside the container) reach your service, which runs on the host.
  • SECRET_<NAME> becomes {{ secret('<NAME>') }} in the flow. The value is base64 (echo -n 'tool-secret-123' | base64). That is how the protected route's token and the webhook key stay out of the YAML.
  • basic-auth turns on API authentication; without credentials it answers 401 (measured in section 5).

Wait for the server to come up and check the version:

curl -s -u admin@example.com:Kestra12345! localhost:18080/api/v1/configs

{"uuid":"2lrxrR7eSFQ8QtCWti1TDa","version":"2.0.6","edition":"OSS","commitId":"b59444f", ...

Pin the image version

The latest-slim tag points to a nightly (the org.opencontainers.image.version label of the image I pulled said nightly). Use v2.0.6-slim, or whichever you validate.

docs.title: 2. The tenant path (measured)
docs.text:
Kestra's documentation is inconsistent: some examples use /api/v1/main/..., others /api/v1/.... Measured on 2.0.6, with Basic Auth:

Call With /main Without /main GET /flows/search 200 200 POST /executions/{namespace}/{flow} 200 200 POST /executions/webhook/{namespace}/{flow}/{key} 200 200 GET /outputs/executions/{id} 200 400 GET /configs 404 200

The 400 says why, and it holds for any segment that is not main:

{"type":"https://kestra.io/docs/api-reference/problems/bad-request","title":"Bad request","status":400,"detail":"Tenant must be 'main' for OSS version", ...

The 400 for /api/v1/outputs/executions/<id> is the same one a tenant other than main gets, which suggests that, without the segment, outputs was read as the tenant. Some routes tolerate the omission, others do not — so always use /api/v1/main/... on tenant routes. The only measured exception is /api/v1/configs, which only answered without /main.

docs.title: 3. The service
docs.text:
A single file with everything the next sections use: the tool route the flow calls, the callback the flow sends when it finishes, and the order that writes the order and the event in the same transaction.

kestra_service.py
import asyncio
import os
from collections.abc import AsyncGenerator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager, suppress
from typing import Annotated, Any
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    AsyncDatabaseManager,
    BaseModel,
    BaseOutboxModel,
    BaseRepository,
    BaseSchema,
    BaseWebhookEventModel,
    HTTPClient,
    OutboxRelay,
    WebhookInbox,
    make_token_dependency,
    register_exception_handlers,
)

TOKEN_SECRET: str = os.environ.get("TOKEN_SECRET", "tool-secret-123")
KESTRA_URL: str = os.environ.get("KESTRA_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:18080")
KESTRA_WEBHOOK_PATH: str = os.environ.get(
    "KESTRA_WEBHOOK_PATH",
    "/api/v1/main/executions/webhook/tempest/order_created/hook-key-abc123",
)

db: AsyncDatabaseManager = AsyncDatabaseManager("sqlite+aiosqlite:///./kestra_demo.db")
require_token = make_token_dependency(TOKEN_SECRET)
Session = Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(db.session_dependency)]


class OrderModel(BaseModel):
    """Service order."""

    __tablename__ = "orders"

    reference: Mapped[str] = mapped_column()
    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(default="created")


class OutboxModel(BaseOutboxModel):
    """Events waiting to be delivered to Kestra."""

    __tablename__ = "outbox"


class WebhookEventModel(BaseWebhookEventModel):
    """Callbacks received from Kestra, deduplicated per execution."""

    __tablename__ = "webhook_events"


class OrderCreateSchema(BaseSchema):
    """Body of `POST /api/orders`."""

    reference: str


class EnrichRequestSchema(BaseSchema):
    """Body the flow sends to the tool route."""

    order_id: str
    source: str


class CallbackSchema(BaseSchema):
    """Body the flow sends when it finishes."""

    execution_id: str
    order_id: str
    enriched: dict[str, Any]


inbox: WebhookInbox[WebhookEventModel] = WebhookInbox(
    db, model=WebhookEventModel, backoff_base_seconds=1.0
)
kestra: HTTPClient = HTTPClient(base_url=KESTRA_URL, timeout=15.0)


async def publish(event: BaseOutboxModel) -> None:
    """Deliver an outbox event to Kestra's webhook.

    Args:
        event (BaseOutboxModel): The outbox row.

    Raises:
        httpx.HTTPStatusError: If Kestra does not answer 2xx; the relay schedules a retry.
    """
    response = await kestra.post(KESTRA_WEBHOOK_PATH, json=event.payload)
    response.raise_for_status()


async def apply_callback(event: WebhookEventModel, session: AsyncSession) -> None:
    """Apply Kestra's callback: mark the order as enriched.

    Args:
        event (WebhookEventModel): The claimed event.
        session (AsyncSession): The session of the transaction that also closes the row.
    """
    order = await session.get(OrderModel, UUID(event.payload["order_id"]))
    if order is not None:
        order.status = "enriched"


async def loop_forever(step: Any) -> None:
    """Run `step()` every half second until cancelled.

    Args:
        step (Any): Coroutine function without arguments to repeat.
    """
    while True:
        await step()
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncGenerator[None, None]:
    """Create the tables, start the outbox relay and the inbox sweep."""
    await db.connect()
    await db.create_tables()
    relay = OutboxRelay(db, model=OutboxModel, publish=publish, backoff_base_seconds=1.0)

    async def sweep() -> None:
        await inbox.drain_once(apply_callback)

    tasks = [
        asyncio.create_task(relay.run(poll_interval=0.5)),
        asyncio.create_task(loop_forever(sweep)),
    ]
    yield
    for task in tasks:
        task.cancel()
    for task in tasks:
        with suppress(asyncio.CancelledError):
            await task
    await kestra.aclose()
    await db.disconnect()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
register_exception_handlers(app)


@app.post("/api/orders", status_code=201)
async def create_order(data: OrderCreateSchema, session: Session) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Create the order and the `orders.created` event in the same transaction."""
    repo: BaseRepository[OrderModel] = BaseRepository(session, model=OrderModel)
    order_id = uuid4()
    event = OutboxModel.new_event(
        "orders.created", {"order_id": str(order_id), "reference": data.reference}
    )
    order = await repo.save_with_outbox(
        OrderModel(id=order_id, reference=data.reference), event
    )
    return {"id": str(order.id), "status": order.status}


@app.get("/api/orders/{order_id}")
async def get_order(order_id: UUID, session: Session) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Return the order's current state."""
    order = await BaseRepository(session, model=OrderModel).get_by_id(order_id)
    return {"id": str(order.id), "status": order.status}


@app.post("/api/tools/enrich-order", dependencies=[Depends(require_token)])
async def enrich_order(data: EnrichRequestSchema) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Tool route the flow calls, protected by `X-Token`."""
    return {"order_id": data.order_id, "caller": data.source, "tier": "gold"}


@app.post("/api/callbacks/kestra", dependencies=[Depends(require_token)])
async def kestra_callback(data: CallbackSchema) -> dict[str, bool]:
    """Record the callback in the inbox and answer 200, even for a repeat."""
    new_id = await inbox.record(
        "kestra", data.execution_id, "flow.finished", data.model_dump()
    )
    return {"recorded": new_id is not None}

Piece by piece:

  • make_token_dependency(TOKEN_SECRET) compares the X-Token header with hmac.compare_digest. The tool route and the callback share the same dependency; POST /api/orders stays open because the service itself is the one calling it.
  • create_order writes OrderModel and the outbox row in one transaction (save_with_outbox) — see the outbox recipe.
  • publish is the publish(event) adapter OutboxRelay requires: a single argument, and raise_for_status() so a non-2xx becomes a retry.
  • kestra_callback writes to the WebhookInbox keyed by (provider, external_id) and answers 200 even for a repeat — the sender only needs to stop retrying. The external_id is Kestra's execution id.
  • apply_callback runs inside the transaction that also marks the inbox row as processed.

Start the service (bound to 0.0.0.0 here because the caller is a container, a separate origin):

uvicorn kestra_service:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 18000

Check the tool route's protection, with and without the token:

curl -s -X POST localhost:18000/api/tools/enrich-order \
  -H 'X-Token: tool-secret-123' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"order_id":"1","source":"curl"}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:18000/api/tools/enrich-order \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"order_id":"1","source":"curl"}' -w ' %{http_code}\n'

{"order_id":"1","caller":"curl","tier":"gold"}
{"detail":"Invalid or missing token","code":"UNAUTHORIZED","details":{}} 401

docs.title: 4. The flows
docs.text:
Two flows, both calling the protected route with the token coming from secret(...). The first is started through the execution API, with an input:

flows/report.yml
id: report
namespace: tempest

inputs:
  - id: order_id
    type: STRING

tasks:
  - id: enrich
    type: io.kestra.plugin.core.http.Request
    uri: http://host.docker.internal:18000/api/tools/enrich-order
    method: POST
    contentType: application/json
    headers:
      X-Token: "{{ secret('SERVICE_TOKEN') }}"
    body: |
      {"order_id": "{{ inputs.order_id }}", "source": "kestra"}

outputs:
  - id: enriched
    type: STRING
    value: "{{ outputs.enrich.body }}"

The second is started by webhook; the body arrives in trigger.body, and the trigger's key also comes from a secret. When it finishes it notifies the service (callback), sending execution.id — the id the inbox uses to deduplicate:

flows/order_created.yml
id: order_created
namespace: tempest

tasks:
  - id: enrich
    type: io.kestra.plugin.core.http.Request
    uri: http://host.docker.internal:18000/api/tools/enrich-order
    method: POST
    contentType: application/json
    headers:
      X-Token: "{{ secret('SERVICE_TOKEN') }}"
    body: |
      {"order_id": "{{ trigger.body.order_id }}", "source": "kestra"}

  - id: callback
    type: io.kestra.plugin.core.http.Request
    uri: http://host.docker.internal:18000/api/callbacks/kestra
    method: POST
    contentType: application/json
    headers:
      X-Token: "{{ secret('SERVICE_TOKEN') }}"
    body: |
      {
        "execution_id": "{{ execution.id }}",
        "order_id": "{{ trigger.body.order_id }}",
        "enriched": {{ outputs.enrich.body }}
      }

outputs:
  - id: callback_status
    type: STRING
    value: "{{ outputs.callback.code }}"

triggers:
  - id: webhook
    type: io.kestra.plugin.core.trigger.Webhook
    key: "{{ secret('WEBHOOK_KEY') }}"

Import both (on 2.0.6 the response was 200):

curl -s -u admin@example.com:Kestra12345! -X POST localhost:18080/api/v1/main/flows \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-yaml' --data-binary @flows/report.yml -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n'
curl -s -u admin@example.com:Kestra12345! -X POST localhost:18080/api/v1/main/flows \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-yaml' --data-binary @flows/order_created.yml -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n'

200
200

docs.title: 5. Trigger from the service
docs.text:
kestra_trigger.py
import asyncio
from base64 import b64encode
from typing import Any

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import HTTPClient, RetryPolicy

TENANT: str = "main"


def make_kestra_client(base_url: str, username: str, password: str) -> HTTPClient:
    """Build the Kestra client with Basic Auth, retry and circuit breaker.

    Args:
        base_url (str): Kestra root, without a trailing slash.
        username (str): Basic Auth user.
        password (str): Basic Auth password.

    Returns:
        HTTPClient: Client ready for the API and the webhooks.
    """
    credentials: str = b64encode(f"{username}:{password}".encode()).decode()
    return HTTPClient(
        base_url=base_url,
        timeout=30.0,
        retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3),
        default_headers={"Authorization": f"Basic {credentials}"},
    )


async def trigger_webhook(
    client: HTTPClient,
    namespace: str,
    flow_id: str,
    key: str,
    payload: dict[str, Any],
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Trigger a flow through its Webhook trigger.

    Args:
        client (HTTPClient): The Kestra client.
        namespace (str): Flow namespace.
        flow_id (str): Flow id.
        key (str): The trigger's `key`; it is the webhook's only check.
        payload (dict[str, Any]): JSON body, which the flow reads in `trigger.body`.

    Returns:
        dict[str, Any]: The created execution (`id`, `state`, ...).

    Raises:
        httpx.HTTPStatusError: If Kestra does not answer 2xx.
    """
    response = await client.post(
        f"/api/v1/{TENANT}/executions/webhook/{namespace}/{flow_id}/{key}",
        json=payload,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return dict(response.json())


async def start_execution(
    client: HTTPClient,
    namespace: str,
    flow_id: str,
    inputs: dict[str, str],
    *,
    wait: bool = False,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Create an execution through the API, with the flow's inputs.

    Args:
        client (HTTPClient): The Kestra client.
        namespace (str): Flow namespace.
        flow_id (str): Flow id.
        inputs (dict[str, str]): Flow inputs; sent as `multipart/form-data`.
        wait (bool): Hold the connection until the execution finishes.

    Returns:
        dict[str, Any]: The execution (`id`, `state`, ...).

    Raises:
        httpx.HTTPStatusError: If Kestra does not answer 2xx.
    """
    response = await client.post(
        f"/api/v1/{TENANT}/executions/{namespace}/{flow_id}",
        params={"wait": str(wait).lower()},
        files={name: (None, value) for name, value in inputs.items()},
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return dict(response.json())


async def read_outputs(client: HTTPClient, execution_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Read the flow outputs of a finished execution.

    Args:
        client (HTTPClient): The Kestra client.
        execution_id (str): Execution id.

    Returns:
        dict[str, Any]: The outputs declared under `outputs:` in the flow.

    Raises:
        httpx.HTTPStatusError: If Kestra does not answer 2xx.
    """
    response = await client.get(f"/api/v1/{TENANT}/outputs/executions/{execution_id}")
    response.raise_for_status()
    return dict(response.json())


async def main() -> None:
    """Call the webhook and the API against a local Kestra and print the result."""
    client = make_kestra_client("http://127.0.0.1:18080", "admin@example.com", "Kestra12345!")
    try:
        created = await trigger_webhook(
            client, "tempest", "order_created", "hook-key-abc123", {"order_id": "demo-1"}
        )
        print("webhook:", created["id"], created["state"]["current"])

        execution = await start_execution(
            client, "tempest", "report", {"order_id": "demo-2"}, wait=True
        )
        print("api:", execution["id"], execution["state"]["current"])
