        print("outputs:", await read_outputs(client, execution["id"]))
    finally:
        await client.aclose()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

python kestra_trigger.py

webhook: 49vM41z1Hsqrd2r0umfjdl CREATED
api: 2EvSyvxiQWdVrzX3Co2MqN SUCCESS
outputs: {'enriched': '{"order_id":"demo-2","caller":"kestra","tier":"gold"}'}

What the measurement showed, and what changes how you write the client:

  • The webhook answers immediately, with the freshly created execution (state.current = CREATED); the flow keeps running behind it. To learn the result, use the callback from section 6 — or ?wait=true on the API.
  • The key is the webhook's only check. A call without Basic Auth, with just the right URL, got 200; with the wrong key it got 404 ("detail":"Webhook not found"). Treat the key as a secret (that is why it comes from secret('WEBHOOK_KEY')) and use a long one.
  • The execution API takes inputs as multipart/form-data. -d order_id=44 (urlencoded) got 415 with Content Type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded] not allowed. Allowed types: [multipart/form-data]. That is why start_execution uses httpx's files={name: (None, value)}, which forces multipart without attaching a file.
  • Without credentials the API answers 401.
  • wait=true holds the connection and returns the finished execution (SUCCESS); without it the state comes back as RUNNING.
  • The flow outputs are not in the execution JSON (the outputs field is absent on 2.0.6). They come from GET /api/v1/main/outputs/executions/{id}, which is what read_outputs calls.

docs.title: 6. Guaranteed delivery: outbox → Kestra, inbox ← Kestra
docs.text:
Create an order. The service answers 201 and does not wait for Kestra:

curl -s -X POST localhost:18000/api/orders -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"reference":"PED-001"}'
sleep 1
curl -s localhost:18000/api/orders/a88f7992-d764-4415-b2da-a045d7ee6647

{"id":"a88f7992-d764-4415-b2da-a045d7ee6647","status":"created"}
{"id":"a88f7992-d764-4415-b2da-a045d7ee6647","status":"enriched"}

In the service log, the full order — the relay delivered the event, the flow called the tool route with the token and then the callback:

INFO:     127.0.0.1:47757 - "POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1" 201 Created
INFO:     172.17.0.2:58240 - "POST /api/tools/enrich-order HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
INFO:     172.17.0.2:58254 - "POST /api/callbacks/kestra HTTP/1.1" 200 OK

docs.title: Kestra down
docs.text:
With the container frozen (docker pause lab-kestra), a new order answers 201 all the same. Twenty-five seconds later, the outbox row is still pending and the order created; unfrozen (docker unpause lab-kestra), the row becomes sent and the order enriched:

{"id":"906c4c47-21b4-486f-af8d-6e308d53b19d","status":"created"}
('orders.created', 'pending', 0, None)          # the new order's row, frozen, 25 s later
{"id":"906c4c47-21b4-486f-af8d-6e308d53b19d","status":"created"}
('orders.created', 'sent', 0)                   # after the unpause
{"id":"906c4c47-21b4-486f-af8d-6e308d53b19d","status":"enriched"}

What this test measures and what it does not

docker pause freezes the process; the connection hangs instead of being refused, and at 25 s the relay had not yet recorded a failure (attempts still 0). This test shows the event waits, durable, in the table and goes out when Kestra is back. The path with attempts climbing, last_error and exponential backoff is the one for fast failures, described in the outbox recipe.

docs.title: The repeated callback
docs.text:
The inbox answers 200 and stores once. Two deliveries with the same execution_id:

{"recorded":true}
{"recorded":false}

('kestra', 'dup-1', 'received')     # a single row, before the sweep processed it

It is at-least-once in both directions

The outbox may publish the same event twice (worker killed between the send and the commit), so the flow may run twice for the same order. Make the flow idempotent on trigger.body.order_id, or keep the order's idempotency key. On our side, the inbox already deduplicates the callback by (provider, external_id).

docs.title: Tear the environment down
docs.text: docker rm -f lab-kestra

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Service → Kestra: HTTPClient + POST /api/v1/main/executions/webhook/{ns}/{flow}/{key} (immediate answer, the key is the only check) or POST /api/v1/main/executions/{ns}/{flow} with multipart/form-data (?wait=true to wait).
  • Tenant: always use /api/v1/main/...; on 2.0.6 any other segment gets 400, and omitting /main only works on some routes.
  • Kestra → service: http.Request task with X-Token: "{{ secret('...') }}" against a route with make_token_dependency.
  • Guaranteed delivery: save_with_outbox + OutboxRelay on the way out; WebhookInbox.record keyed by the execution id on the way back.
  • No new module: all of this is HTTPClient, make_token_dependency, OutboxRelay and WebhookInbox.

docs.title: Storage on local disk — LocalObjectStorageClient
docs.text:
Your service keeps photos, exports and attachments, and until now that meant an S3 server (MinIO, AWS, R2) running beside the API. For a service that runs on one machine, that server is one more piece to start, upgrade and watch.

LocalObjectStorageClient keeps the objects in a directory of the server itself and answers the same calls as AsyncMinIOClient — put_object, stat_object, stream_object, list_objects, remove_object, remove_objects, presigned_get_url, presigned_put_url. The rest of the service does not change.

What changes is the link. A disk has no endpoint the browser can reach, so the "presigned" link points at your API, signed with sign_path, and make_local_storage_router serves those routes.

No extra needed: only the standard library and the FastAPI the SDK already brings. The optional encryption at rest needs [storage-encryption].

docs.title: The first object
docs.text:
import asyncio
from datetime import timedelta

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalObjectStorageClient


async def main() -> None:
    """Write, describe, read and sign an object on disk."""
    storage = LocalObjectStorageClient(
        "var/storage",
        public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
        signing_secret="replace-with-a-long-secret",
    )
    etag = await storage.put_object(
        "reports/2026.txt",
        b"conteudo",
        content_type="text/plain",
    )
    stat = await storage.stat_object("reports/2026.txt")
    stream = await storage.stream_object("reports/2026.txt")
    body = b"".join([chunk async for chunk in stream])
    link = await storage.presigned_get_url(
        "reports/2026.txt", expires=timedelta(minutes=10)
    )
    print(etag, stat.size, stat.content_type, body)
    print(link)


asyncio.run(main())

Running it prints something like:

b59853db2f3ef8f156a72e38c30ba7d2 8 text/plain b'conteudo'
http://127.0.0.1:8000/storage/uploads/reports/2026.txt?expires=1792869637&signature=tvsYmCeLaH3y...

Piece by piece:

  • "var/storage" is the root. The client creates objects/, meta/ and tmp/ inside it.
  • The default bucket is "uploads" (default_bucket=). Each bucket is a subfolder of objects/.
  • put_object returns the ETag, the MD5 of the bytes, as S3 answers for a single-part upload.
  • stat_object reads size and date from the file, and content type and metadata from the metadata file stored beside it.
  • The link lasts 10 minutes and only opens that object's route.

What it looks like on disk

var/storage/
  objects/uploads/reports/2026.txt          the bytes
  meta/uploads/reports/2026.txt.meta.json   content type, metadata, ETag
  tmp/                                      writes in flight
Every write goes to tmp/ first and is moved into place with os.replace. A reader sees the old object or the new one, never half of one.

docs.title: Serving the links from the API
docs.text:
The link points at <public_url><route_prefix>/<bucket>/<key>. Mount the router at the app root, with no extra prefix: the signature covers the path the app sees, and the router already carries the client's route_prefix.

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    LocalObjectStorageClient,
    make_local_storage_router,
    register_exception_handlers,
)

storage = LocalObjectStorageClient(
    "var/storage",
    public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    signing_secret="replace-with-a-long-secret",
    route_prefix="/api/storage",
    max_upload_bytes=5 * 1024 * 1024,
)

app = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)
app.include_router(make_local_storage_router(storage))


@app.get("/api/photos/{name}")
async def photo_link(name: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Return a 15-minute link to the photo (authorize first)."""
    return {"url": await storage.presigned_get_url(f"photos/{name}")}


@app.post("/api/photos/{name}/upload-url")
async def upload_link(name: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Return a direct upload link for the photo."""
    return {"url": await storage.presigned_put_url(f"photos/{name}")}

The two routes the router mounts:

Route What it does GET /api/storage/{bucket}/{key} checks the download signature and serves the file with its stored content type, with Range (206), If-None-Match (304) and 416 PUT /api/storage/{bucket}/{key} checks the upload signature and stores the raw body with the request's Content-Type; answers 200 with the ETag

The app's client uploads like this, with no token: the link is the credential.

curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: image/jpeg" --data-binary @photo.jpg "<upload url>"

Download and upload do not mix

GET and PUT links are signed for different purposes. A download link used in a PUT answers 403 SIGNED_URL_INVALID and stores nothing, and the other way round too.

The router's error responses:

Situation Response no signature, tampered signature, or another purpose 403 SIGNED_URL_INVALID expired link 403 SIGNED_URL_EXPIRED object that does not exist (download) 404 NOT_FOUND body over max_upload_bytes 413 FILE_TOO_LARGE, leaving no file

The cap holds even without Content-Length: the body is counted as it arrives and cut when it passes the limit.

The payload is not signed

As with S3, the upload link only fixes where the file goes, not what it is. Check size and type with stat_object (and the first bytes with stream_object) before trusting the object.

docs.title: Capped upload and download with a signed type
docs.text:
The two S3 features the plain PUT and GET lack exist here under the same call, so the service switches backend without touching the app's client.

presigned_post_policy returns a PresignedPost (URL + form fields). The POST /api/storage/{bucket}/{key} route reads the multipart/form-data and applies the signed limits before storing:

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    LocalObjectStorageClient,
    make_local_storage_router,
    register_exception_handlers,
)

storage = LocalObjectStorageClient(
    "var/storage",
    public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    signing_secret="replace-with-a-long-secret",
    route_prefix="/api/storage",
    max_upload_bytes=5 * 1024 * 1024,
)

app = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)
app.include_router(make_local_storage_router(storage))


@app.post("/api/photos/{name}/form")
async def upload_form(name: str) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Form that accepts only JPEG up to 2 MiB."""
    post = await storage.presigned_post_policy(
        f"photos/{name}",
        max_bytes=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_type="image/jpeg",
    )
    return {"url": post.url, "fields": post.fields}


@app.get("/api/photos/{name}/inline")
async def inline_link(name: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Link that opens the photo inline, as JPEG."""
    url = await storage.presigned_get_url(
        f"photos/{name}",
        media_type="image/jpeg",
        as_attachment=False,
    )
    return {"url": url}
POST case Answer file within [min_bytes, max_bytes] 204, with the ETag over max_bytes 413 FILE_TOO_LARGE, nothing stored under min_bytes 400 FILE_TOO_SMALL, nothing stored Content-Type or key field other than the signed one 403 SIGNED_URL_INVALID max_bytes (or another limit) edited in the URL 403 SIGNED_URL_INVALID

The limits and the GET overrides travel in the query, and the SDK binds them to the signature (bound_purpose): changing one verifies as another purpose and fails. A link signed with none of them still works as before.

Needs the [upload] extra

Reading the form takes python-multipart. The check runs in presigned_post_policy, so a missing extra breaks where the link is issued, not on the user's upload.

max_bytes up to max_upload_bytes

The form's cap cannot exceed the store's: asking for more raises ValueError when signing.

docs.title: Picking the backend from settings
docs.text:
StorageSettings picks between S3 and disk with STORAGE_BACKEND, and build_storage_client() builds the right client:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    AsyncMinIOClient,
    BaseAppSettings,
    LocalObjectStorageClient,
    StorageSettings,
)


class Settings(StorageSettings, BaseAppSettings):
    """The service's settings."""


settings = Settings()
client: AsyncMinIOClient | LocalObjectStorageClient = settings.build_storage_client()

STORAGE_BACKEND=local
STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR=/var/lib/app/storage
STORAGE_LOCAL_PUBLIC_URL=https://api.example.com
STORAGE_LOCAL_ROUTE_PREFIX=/api/storage
STORAGE_LOCAL_SIGNING_SECRET=a-long-random-secret
STORAGE_LOCAL_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES=5242880
STORAGE_DEFAULT_BUCKET=media
Variable Default What for STORAGE_BACKEND s3 local turns the disk on STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR var/storage the store's root STORAGE_LOCAL_PUBLIC_URL http://127.0.0.1:8000 start of the links STORAGE_LOCAL_ROUTE_PREFIX /storage path of the routes, as the app sees it STORAGE_LOCAL_SIGNING_SECRET dev placeholder secret of the links STORAGE_LOCAL_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES 25 MiB PUT cap

With ENV=production (EnvironmentSettings) and STORAGE_BACKEND=local, the boot refuses the development secret, a STORAGE_LOCAL_PUBLIC_URL without https and a relative STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR. The S3 credentials are no longer checked, because nothing reads them.

Reusing JWT_SECRET

The signature derives its key from the secret and the purpose, so putting the JWT_SECRET value in STORAGE_LOCAL_SIGNING_SECRET is safe: a link never works as a token, and the other way round.

docs.title: With SubjectObjectStorage
docs.text:
The local client satisfies SubjectStorageClient, so per-subject export and erasure (LGPD) work the same:

import asyncio

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalObjectStorageClient
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.privacy import SubjectObjectStorage


async def main() -> None:
    """Store two files of a subject and erase them all at once."""
    client = LocalObjectStorageClient(
        "var/storage",
        public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
        signing_secret="replace-with-a-long-secret",
    )
    storage = SubjectObjectStorage(client, prefix="users")
    await storage.put(42, "avatar.png", b"png", content_type="image/png")
    await storage.put(42, "export.json", b"{}", content_type="application/json")
    print(await storage.names(42))
    print(await storage.delete_all(42))


asyncio.run(main())

['avatar.png', 'export.json']
2

A missing object raises LocalObjectNotFoundError, a FileNotFoundError with code = "NoSuchKey" — the code S3 answers. Code that branches on the S3 error's code keeps working.

docs.title: Encryption at rest
docs.text:
So far the files sit in plaintext on the disk. If your service keeps a photo of an ID, of a notebook or anything personal, whoever reaches the disk, a snapshot of the volume or a backup of it reads everything — even when the database encrypts its content columns.

The bytes come in and go out through paths the SDK owns (the signed PUT/POST the app calls directly, the signed GET, download_response), so the encryption lives in the client: pass encryption_keys and every write path encrypts, every read path decrypts. The rest of the service does not change.

docs.title: Generating the key
docs.text:
Each key is 32 bytes (AES-256). Generate one in base64:

python -c "import os,base64;print(base64.b64encode(os.urandom(32)).decode())"

2yk6fNE3HpXOhHypqJSA3ncp6UWjTI/4jORNYXz2RDo=

And install the extra that brings the cipher (cryptography):

uv add "tempest-fastapi-sdk[storage-encryption]"

docs.title: The first encrypted object
docs.text:
import asyncio
import os

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LocalObjectStorageClient


async def main() -> None:
    """Store an encrypted object, look at the disk and read it back."""
    storage = LocalObjectStorageClient(
        "var/storage",
        public_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
        signing_secret="change-me-to-a-long-secret",
        encryption_keys={"2026-11": os.urandom(32)},
    )
    await storage.put_object(
        "notebooks/photo.jpg",
        b"notebook contents",
        content_type="image/jpeg",
    )
    on_disk = storage.object_path("notebooks/photo.jpg").read_bytes()
    stat = await storage.stat_object("notebooks/photo.jpg")
    stream = await storage.stream_object("notebooks/photo.jpg")
    body = b"".join([chunk async for chunk in stream])
    print(on_disk[:8], b"notebook" in on_disk, len(on_disk))
    print(stat.size, body)


asyncio.run(main())

b'TFSDKENC' False 57
17 b'notebook contents'

Piece by piece:

  • encryption_keys is a dictionary of id → key. The id is written in every file's header; the key, never.
  • The file on disk starts with the TFSDKENC marker and does not hold the text: 57 bytes for 17 of content (header + a 16-byte tag per block).
  • stat_object answers the plaintext size (17), which is what you compare against an upload cap.
  • stream_object returns the original bytes.

The example's key dies with the process

os.urandom(32) in code is there to watch the cipher work. In a service the key comes from the environment (see the settings below): without it, nothing that was written opens again.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The file is cut into 64 KiB blocks (LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_BLOCK_SIZE) and each block is sealed with AES-256-GCM, from cryptography. It is the STREAM construction:

  • each block's nonce is a random per-file prefix + the block number + a "last block" flag;
  • the header (format version, key id, prefix) and the object's <bucket>/<key> are authenticated data.

So writes and reads keep streaming, without loading the whole file, and every tampering turns into an error:

What happened to the file Result a byte changed in the content, a tag or the nonce prefix StorageIntegrityException, reason="authentication" unknown version or header cut short reason="format" blocks out of order reason="authentication" last block removed reason="authentication" cut inside a tag reason="format" copied or renamed to another key or bucket reason="authentication" sealed with a key the client does not hold reason="unknown_key" a plaintext file, without allow_plaintext_read reason="plaintext"

StorageIntegrityException is an AppException with status 500 and code="STORAGE_INTEGRITY_ERROR". Its details carry the reason only — never the object's name or any byte of it.

No unauthenticated byte

Each block is handed out only after its tag verified. The first block is checked before stream_object returns the stream, so through the router a tampered file answers a clean 500 STORAGE_INTEGRITY_ERROR. If a block in the middle fails, the response has already started: the connection is cut after the blocks that verified (measured with uvicorn and httpx: 200, two 64 KiB blocks received, then RemoteProtocolError for the missing rest of the Content-Length).

docs.title: Through the API, nothing changes
docs.text:
make_local_storage_router keeps its shape:

  • the signed PUT and POST store encrypted; the cap (max_upload_bytes, max_bytes) counts the content, not the header and the tags;
  • the signed GET serves plaintext, with the content's Content-Length;
  • Range works: the client decrypts only the blocks the range covers. SubjectObjectStorage.read(..., max_bytes=...) also stops at the limit and decrypts nothing past it.

docs.title: From settings
docs.text:
STORAGE_BACKEND=local
STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS='{"2026-11":"2yk6fNE3HpXOhHypqJSA3ncp6UWjTI/4jORNYXz2RDo="}'
Variable Default What for STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS {} JSON of id → base64 key; the first writes, all read STORAGE_LOCAL_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_READ false reads an old file without a header as plaintext (during the migration only)

local_storage_kwargs() decodes the keys and passes encryption_keys and allow_plaintext_read to the client, so build_storage_client() comes out encrypting. Without keys the dictionary is the one it always was. A key that is not the base64 of 32 bytes fails the boot with its id in the message, never its value.

Production without a key: a warning, not a refusal

With ENV=production, STORAGE_BACKEND=local and no key, the boot goes on and logs a WARNING on the tempest_fastapi_sdk.settings logger. Refusing would break, without notice, every service that already runs the local backend in production on the day it upgrades. Switch the encryption on and the warning goes away.

docs.title: Migrating a volume that already has files
docs.text:
A file written before the key has no header. With the key on it is refused (reason="plaintext"), unless you allow plaintext reads during the migration:

  1. Generate the key and deploy with both variables:

    STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS='{"2026-11":"<base64>"}'
STORAGE_LOCAL_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_READ=true

    From here on, every new file is written encrypted, and the old ones keep opening.

  2. Encrypt what exists, ideally in a window without writes:

    tempest storage encrypt-local

    docs: 1 object(s) encrypted
uploads: 1 object(s) encrypted

    The command walks every bucket of STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR (--bucket limits it to one) and is idempotent: an encrypted file is skipped, so running it again after an interruption rewrites nothing. Content type and metadata stay; the ETag becomes the MD5 of the encrypted file.

  3. Remove STORAGE_LOCAL_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_READ and restart.

In code the same is await storage.encrypt_existing() (per bucket, with await storage.list_buckets()).

Writes during the migration

Each file is rewritten in tmp/ and only swapped in if it did not change while it was read (same inode, size and time). The check and the swap are two steps, so a write landing exactly between them is lost. Run it with the service stopped or with no upload in flight.

docs.title: Rotating the key
docs.text:
The first key of the JSON writes; any key reads, by the header's id:

  1. Put the new key first and keep the old one:

    STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS='{"2027-05":"<new>","2026-11":"<old>"}'

    New writes go out under 2027-05; what is under 2026-11 keeps opening.

  2. Rewrite what is under the old key:

    tempest storage reencrypt-local

    Idempotent too: what is already under the first key is skipped. A file that does not decrypt (its key left the ring, the file is damaged) stops the command with the error and exit code 1, rewriting nothing of it. In code: await storage.reencrypt().

  3. Remove the old key from the JSON.

docs.title: What the encryption protects, and what it does not
docs.text:
It protects the files at rest: the disk, a snapshot of the volume, a backup copied elsewhere, a volume mounted by mistake on another machine.

It does not protect:

  • a compromised process. The API decrypts to serve; whoever runs code in it reads what it reads.
  • the key next to the data. A key in the .env that travels with the volume in the same backup is a padlock with the key hanging from it. Keep it in a secrets manager, or at least out of the volume and its backup.
  • what leaked before the migration. Old backups and snapshots stay in plaintext, and the disk may keep the freed blocks of the old file. Rotate the old backups out of retention.
  • the metadata. The key name (<bucket>/<key>), content type, user metadata and the approximate size stay visible on disk.

One key per environment

Development, staging and production with different keys: a production backup restored by mistake elsewhere does not open.

docs.title: Before going to production
docs.text:
One machine only

The disk belongs to one server. Two API instances on different machines do not see each other's files. Once you scale past one machine, go back to S3 (STORAGE_BACKEND=s3).

API and worker on the same volume

Processes on the same machine share the store by mounting the same directory. In docker compose, that is a named volume mounted at the same path in the API and in the worker:

services:
  api:
    volumes:
      - storage:/var/lib/app/storage
  worker:
    volumes:
      - storage:/var/lib/app/storage

volumes:
  storage:

Backup is yours

Managed S3 replicates the data; a directory does not. Add STORAGE_LOCAL_DIR (with objects/ and meta/) to the server's backup routine.

Technical details
  • Every blocking call runs in asyncio.to_thread.
  • An empty key, one starting with /, with a . or .. segment, with \ or NUL, or with a segment ending in .meta.json is refused with ValueError. The final path is resolved (following symlinks) and must stay under the root.
  • On a disk, keys a and a/b cannot coexist (a cannot be a file and a folder at once); writing the second raises OSError (FileExistsError or IsADirectoryError, depending on the order). S3 accepts both.
  • list_objects(recursive=False) returns "folders" ending in /, as S3 does. A prefix whose directory part has an empty, . or .. segment, or that resolves outside the bucket (a symlink included), returns [] — on S3 ../ is just characters no key starts with.
  • remove_objects returns AccessDenied for a permission error and InternalError for anything else, one ObjectDeleteError per key.
  • X-Accel-Redirect is not supported by the local client: GET always goes through the API.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• LocalObjectStorageClient keeps objects in a directory and speaks the same language as AsyncMinIOClient.
  • The "presigned" links point at the API; make_local_storage_router serves them, at the app root.
  • STORAGE_BACKEND=local + build_storage_client() swap the backend without touching the rest of the service.
  • One machine only, a volume shared by the API and the worker, a backup of the directory.
  • encryption_keys (STORAGE_LOCAL_ENCRYPTION_KEYS) seals each file in AES-256-GCM blocks: the first key writes, all read, and tampering turns into StorageIntegrityException.
  • tempest storage encrypt-local migrates an old volume and tempest storage reencrypt-local closes a rotation; both are idempotent.
  • The encryption protects the disk, snapshots and backups; it does not protect the process or a key kept next to the data.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
In this recipe you set up structured JSON logs with per-request correlation, one file per severity level, and an HTTP endpoint to read them back. The goal is that every log line is parseable, traceable to the request that produced it, and inspectable without SSHing into the server.

configure_logging installs a JSON handler on the root logger that emits one-line JSON records carrying the active request ID. LogUtils is a thin facade that adds level methods accepting structured **fields.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils, configure_logging
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.core import get_request_id

from src.db.models import UserModel


def risky() -> None:
    """Blow up, so the log shows a real traceback."""
    raise RuntimeError("boom")


user = UserModel(email="ana@example.com")


# Imperative — call once during bootstrap.
configure_logging(level="INFO", json_output=True)

# Facade — handy for service-wide singletons.
log = LogUtils("app.users", level="INFO")
log.info("user_created", user_id=str(user.id), email=user.email)
log.warning("login_throttled", ip="1.2.3.4", attempts=5)

try:
    risky()
except RuntimeError:
    log.exception("risky_failed", op="reconcile")  # appends traceback

# Surface the correlation ID outside the log line if needed.
request_id = get_request_id()

Adopting it in a service that already logs %-style

The level methods take logging's positional arguments, so existing call sites move over without a rewrite — and keep lazy interpolation and the stable template a log tool groups on:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils

log = LogUtils("app.email", level="INFO")

log.info("Email sent to %s", "ana@example.com")
log.error("Sending to %s failed: %s", "bruno@x.com", "timeout")

log.error("Sending to %s failed: %s", "bruno@x.com", "timeout", op="send")

The last line shows the two styles coexisting: the positionals build the message, and **fields still becomes top-level keys on the JSON.

funcName/lineno point at your call site, not inside the facade — the default is stacklevel=2. Wrapping LogUtils in a layer of your own? Pass stacklevel=3 (or more) to walk past the extra frames.

JSON output (single line — formatted here for readability):

{
  "timestamp": "2026-05-16T20:14:33.412Z",
  "level": "INFO",
  "logger": "app.users",
  "message": "user_created",
  "request_id": "d83e4b0c-7c2f-4bd6-aaa1-7d4f6cf5e5e9",
  "user_id": "9c1a5b2d-...",
  "email": "ana@example.com"
}

The middleware accepts a custom header name (RequestIDMiddleware(app, header_name="X-Correlation-ID")); the same header is echoed back on every response.

docs.title: One handler set, not one per module
docs.text:
LogUtils(__name__) is how the class reads, and how it gets used: one line at the top of every module. Since v0.280.0 it is also what the class does well.

# src/services/user.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils

logger: LogUtils = LogUtils(__name__)

logger.info("User %s created", "u-1")

# src/services/payment.py
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils

logger: LogUtils = LogUtils(__name__)

logger.warning("Charge %s expired", "c-9")

Both modules write to the same files through the same handler set: the constructor configures the root logger, once per process, and binds __name__ to it by propagation. The logger name still rides on every line (the logger field), so you still know who wrote what.

Why this matters more than it looks

Through v0.279.0 the constructor called configure_logging(logger_name=name), which sets propagate = False on that logger and gives it handlers of its own. Measured: 7 handlers per logger (1 stdout + 6 files), so a service with 27 modules opened 27 stdout and 162 file handlers, all pointed at the same six paths — and RotatingFileHandler does not coordinate rollover across instances: when the file hits the ceiling several of them try to roll the same path, and the result is lost records and interleaved .1/.2 backups.

Measured in a process with five instances: 7 handlers on the root (1 stdout + 6 files) and zero on each module logger.

The first instance decides level and format

"Once per process" has a consequence: the second call reconfigures nothing, so level= and json_output= from the second one on are ignored. That is what you want in a service — the bootstrap decides — but it surprises in tests, where each case wants its own. Call reinitialize_logging() between them.

To isolate one logger on purpose — a subsystem whose stream you do not want merged — ask for the old shape:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils

audit: LogUtils = LogUtils("audit", log_dir="logs/audit", scope="logger")

docs.title: Per-level files + isolated 500.log
docs.text:
By default the SDK writes to stdout AND to logs/ (one JSON file per level) at the same time. Each file receives only its own level (exact match — an ERROR never lands in warning.log), so every severity becomes an isolated, greppable stream.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import configure_logging

# Defaults — stdout + logs/{debug,info,warning,error,critical,500}.log
configure_logging(level="INFO")

# Custom directory
configure_logging(level="INFO", log_dir="/var/log/myapp")

# Disable file output (stdout-only — handy for serverless / read-only FS)
configure_logging(level="INFO", file_output=False)

# Disable stdout (sidecar tails from disk)
configure_logging(level="INFO", stdout=False)

# Growth ceiling: each file rotates at ~10 MB, keeping 5 generations
configure_logging(level="INFO", max_bytes=10_000_000, backup_count=5)

# No rotation — when the host's logrotate (or a sidecar) owns retention
configure_logging(level="INFO", max_bytes=0)

Files rotate by default — here is why

A plain FileHandler grows without bound. On a service that logs one line per request, running on a long-lived host, info.log is what fills the disk — and a full disk takes the service down along with anything else sharing the partition. So the default is a RotatingFileHandler with max_bytes=10_000_000 and backup_count=5: ~60 MB per level, hard cap.

The other half of this pair already had its ceiling: make_logs_router reads at most 20k records per file, added after a service whose log directory had grown to gigabytes answered with a dead worker. This is the writing half.

Rotated files (info.log.1, info.log.2, …) are read by /logs and by the /admin/logs page, together with the current file and inside the same 20k-records-per-level ceiling. Longer retention than that is a collector's job.

Don't disable both

configure_logging(stdout=False, file_output=False) raises ValueError — silencing every handler leaves the application blind.

File logging is best-effort — it never crashes startup

If log_dir cannot be created or its files cannot be opened (read-only filesystem, missing write permission, hardened container, serverless, CI), the SDK skips the file handlers, emits a warning (to the logger when stdout is on, otherwise straight to stderr) and keeps running with stdout only — instead of dying at import with PermissionError: [Errno 13] ... 'logs'. Pass file_output=False to opt out of file logging explicitly.

On disk:

logs/
├── debug.log      # only DEBUG records
├── info.log       # only INFO records
├── warning.log    # only WARNING records
├── error.log      # only ERROR records (a 500 lands here too)
├── critical.log   # only CRITICAL records
└── 500.log        # only uncaught-500 records (isolated)

500s are grave — that's why they get their own file

The catch-all handler registered by register_exception_handlers flags every uncaught exception with the http_500=True extra. configure_logging(log_dir=...) routes those records to a dedicated 500.log in addition to error.log. The gravest failure is never buried among the other errors.

That holds for scope="root", the default. With scope="logger" the root is not configured, the SDK's logger sits outside the tree, and the record reaches neither file — pass register_exception_handlers(app, logger=log.logger) to route it. Measured detail in Telling someone, and choosing where the record lands.

Always in the logs, never in the body

The traceback goes to the files/terminal via logging — not to the response body. A 500 body is just the generic envelope ({"detail": "Internal server error", "code": "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR"}). See HTTP layer for the log_traceback / include_traceback flags.

Files are always JSON

File handlers use JSONFormatter regardless of json_output, so the /logs endpoint can parse them back. json_output only controls the stdout format.

In the scaffold the directory comes from LOG_DIR (defaults to "logs"; set it empty to disable file logging). Add logs/ to your .gitignore.

The LogSettings mixin models the whole configuration, rotation included, and logging_kwargs() hands it over ready to splat — so the field-to-argument translation lives in one place instead of in a hand-written call where the two newest arguments are exactly the ones that get left out:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import configure_logging
from tempest_fastapi_sdk.settings import LogSettings


class Settings(LogSettings):
    """The service's configuration."""


config = Settings()
configure_logging(**config.logging_kwargs())
Variable Default What it decides LOG_LEVEL INFO Minimum level emitted. LOG_JSON True JSON on stdout (files are always JSON). LOG_DIR logs Directory for the files; empty disables file logging. LOG_MAX_BYTES 10000000 Size at which each file rotates; 0 disables rotation. LOG_BACKUP_COUNT 5 Generations kept per level. LOG_ROTATE_WHEN empty Rotate by time (midnight, H, D, W0–W6, S, M); empty keeps size-based rotation. LOG_ROTATE_INTERVAL 1 How many LOG_ROTATE_WHEN units make one period.

The disk budget is LOG_MAX_BYTES * (LOG_BACKUP_COUNT + 1) per level, times the six files — under size-based rotation.

docs.title: Rotate by time — keep one week
docs.text:
A byte ceiling answers "how much disk", not "how much time". When the question is "I want exactly the last week of logs", rotate by time: rotate_when swaps every file handler for a TimedRotatingFileHandler (always UTC), and backup_count starts counting periods.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import configure_logging

configure_logging(
    level="INFO",
    log_dir="logs",
    rotate_when="midnight",
    backup_count=7,
)

From the environment, with the LogSettings of the previous section:

LOG_ROTATE_WHEN=midnight
LOG_BACKUP_COUNT=7

At UTC midnight the day's file becomes a backup named after the period's date, and the oldest one past the seventh is deleted:

logs/
├── info.log              # today
├── info.log.2026-10-19   # yesterday
├── info.log.2026-10-18
│   ...
└── info.log.2026-10-13   # seven days ago — the eighth goes at the next rollover

Checked in tests/core/test_logging_time_rotation.py: ten rollovers in a row with backup_count=7 leave exactly the seven newest days.

rotate_when Period Backup name "S" / "M" / "H" second / minute / hour info.log.2026-10-20_13-05-00 / info.log.2026-10-20_13-05 / info.log.2026-10-20_13 "D" 24 h from startup info.log.2026-10-20 "midnight" day, rolling at UTC midnight info.log.2026-10-20 "W0"–"W6" week, rolling on that day (W0 = Monday) info.log.2026-10-20

rotate_interval multiplies the unit: rotate_when="H", rotate_interval=6 rotates every six hours.

Under time-based rotation, max_bytes is ignored

A period's file is never cut by size: a burst of logging inside one day grows that day's file. If the volume per period is not predictable, prefer size-based rotation (the default) or leave retention to the host's logrotate.

An invalid unit fails at the call, not at the first log

configure_logging(rotate_when="daily") raises ValueError listing the accepted units (validate_rotate_when) before removing the current handlers — and LOG_ROTATE_WHEN=daily fails the boot in Settings validation.

Readers see both backup shapes

read_log_entries, GET /logs and the /admin/logs page read the current file and its backups — info.log.1 or info.log.2026-10-20 — newest first (rotated_log_files). A directory that switched modes keeps showing what the previous mode left behind.

docs.title: Reporting a 500 of your own — error_500
docs.text:
The SDK's catch-all handler marks every unhandled exception with http_500=True, which is what 500.log filters on. When your code detects a grave failure that never becomes an exception — a wallet credit that rolled back, a transfer stranded at the gateway — error_500 puts the record in that same file:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils

logger: LogUtils = LogUtils(__name__)


def settle(charge_id: str) -> None:
    """Credit a wallet, escalating a rollback to the 500 stream."""
    try:
        raise RuntimeError("commit failed")
    except RuntimeError:
        logger.error_500(
            "CRITICAL: wallet credit failed for charge %s",
            charge_id,
            charge_id=charge_id,
        )

The record lands in 500.log and in error.log — the isolated file exists so a grave failure is not buried, not to remove it from the level stream. The traceback rides along whenever one is being handled.

exc_info="auto" for the call site that is sometimes in an except

logger.exception(...) requires being inside an except; exc_info=True outside one writes the useless NoneType: None. A helper called from both places wants the third option:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils

logger: LogUtils = LogUtils(__name__)

logger.error("Failed to send to %s", "ana@x.com", exc_info="auto")

The default stays False, so existing call sites do not change output.

docs.title: An expected 503 is not a failure — log_level on the exception
docs.text:
Every AppException with status_code >= 500 lands in 500.log with a traceback, like a bug. Some 5xx are planned answers, though: the integration the .env switched off (STORAGE_ENABLED=false) answers 503 INTEGRATION_DISABLED on purpose. In a service with storage and AI switched off, 8 of the 11 records in the panel's "500" source were that 503, each with the full traceback, and the one real bug sat among them.

The exception declares its own log severity in the log_level class attribute:

import logging
from typing import ClassVar

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    AppException,
    IntegrationDisabledException,
    register_exception_handlers,
)

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")


class MaintenanceException(AppException):
    """Scheduled maintenance: an expected 503, not a failure."""

    status_code: int = 503
    message: str = "Scheduled maintenance"
    code: str = "MAINTENANCE"
    log_level: ClassVar[int | None] = logging.WARNING


app: FastAPI = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)


@app.get("/files")
async def files() -> None:
    raise IntegrationDisabledException("storage")


@app.get("/report")
async def report() -> None:
    raise MaintenanceException()


client: TestClient = TestClient(app)
print(client.get("/files").status_code)
print(client.get("/report").status_code)

Output (measured; the TestClient's httpx lines are omitted):

WARNING tempest_fastapi_sdk.api.handlers: AppException 503 (INTEGRATION_DISABLED) during GET /files: The storage integration is disabled in this environment
WARNING tempest_fastapi_sdk.api.handlers: AppException 503 (MAINTENANCE) during GET /report: Scheduled maintenance
503
503

With log_level declared, the handler:

  • logs at that level, without a traceback;
  • does not set the http_500 marker, so the record stays out of 500.log and the panel's "500" source (it still lands in warning.log);
  • does not call on_server_error.

The status and the envelope do not change. None, the default, keeps the previous rule. In the SDK, IntegrationDisabledException and EmailDeliveryException (503 EMAIL_UNAVAILABLE) declare logging.WARNING; for the latter, the mailer already logs the SMTP failure at ERROR before raising.

Declare only what is planned

A real-failure 5xx (the upstream went down, the database refused) keeps no log_level: that is the one that needs the traceback and 500.log.

docs.title: The database quotes the value — redact_database_errors
docs.text:
An IntegrityError nobody handled reaches the catch-all, and the traceback that goes to the log ends in the exception's str(). On Postgres that text is the server's sentence, and it quotes the row:

sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError: (sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql.asyncpg.IntegrityError) <class 'asyncpg.exceptions.UniqueViolationError'>: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "p_cpf_key"
DETAIL:  Key (cpf)=(123.456.789-00) already exists.
[SQL: INSERT INTO p (cpf) VALUES ($1)]
[SQL parameters hidden due to hide_parameters=True]
(Background on this error at: https://sqlalche.me/e/20/gkpj)

Look at the parameters line: hide_parameters=True was on. It removes the parameter block SQLAlchemy appends, but the DETAIL line is the server's text, relayed by the driver, and it stays. The CPF the client sent went to error.log, 500.log, GET /logs and the /admin/logs panel.

That is why the three 5xx handlers apply redact_database_errors before they log, by default. With the same error, the last line of the traceback becomes:

tempest_fastapi_sdk.api.redaction.RedactedError: sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError: unique violation; constraint=p_cpf_key; table=p; columns=cpf; driver=sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql.asyncpg.AsyncAdapt_asyncpg_dbapi.IntegrityError; database message withheld from the log

Both outputs above were captured from a real Postgres 16, with the SDK's JSONFormatter, under SQLAlchemy 2.0.52. Under 2.1.1 the summary is the same except for driver=, which ends in AsyncAdapt_asyncpg_dbapi.UniqueViolationError.

  • The frames stay. Every File ..., line ... is the original error's; only the database error's text changes.
  • The schema names stay. Constraint, table and columns come from parse_integrity_error — they are DDL names, not data.
  • The server's text goes entirely, for every DBAPIError, not only IntegrityError: a DataError quotes the rejected input too. The SQL statement goes with it, because a text() built with an f-string carries the literal.
  • Nothing but the log changes. The response is the same 500 envelope, and on_server_error receives the original exception — the Sentry you plug in there still sees everything, and what it keeps is your call.

A 500 with no database error in its chain logs exactly as before: the function returns the same object.

The handled path had the same leak: turning the IntegrityError into a 409, BaseRepository wrote a warning with the driver's text. It now writes IntegrityError on User.add: unique violation; constraint=...; table=...; columns=..., built by describe_database_error — the same function behind the summary above, public for your own except IntegrityError.

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import register_exception_handlers

app: FastAPI = FastAPI()

register_exception_handlers(app)

That is all: the default already protects you. To log the raw exception — locally, reading DETAIL on purpose — pass redact_exception=None. For a policy of your own, pass any (BaseException) -> BaseException callable:

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import redact_database_errors, register_exception_handlers


class PaymentGatewayError(Exception):
    """Gateway error whose message carries the card number."""


def redact(error: BaseException) -> BaseException:
    """Hide the gateway on top of the database."""
    if isinstance(error, PaymentGatewayError):
        return RuntimeError("payment gateway failed; message withheld")
    return redact_database_errors(error)


app: FastAPI = FastAPI()

register_exception_handlers(app, redact_exception=redact)

What the summary leaves out

The driver's exception (asyncpg's UniqueViolationError, and SQLAlchemy's adapter around it) leaves the chain, because its text is the same server sentence. Its type stays in the summary, as driver=....

docs.title: Personal data out of every line — redact=True
docs.text:
A service that handles personal data has to keep e-mails, tokens and verification codes out of every log line — including the ones you did not write: the traceback that quotes the payload, the extra= passed whole, the third-party library that logs the Authorization header. configure_logging handles it with one parameter:

import logging

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import RedactionPolicy, configure_logging

policy: RedactionPolicy = RedactionPolicy(extra_keys={"cpf"})
configure_logging(file_output=False, redact=policy)
log: logging.Logger = logging.getLogger("app.signup")

log.info(
    "code sent to %s",
    "ana@example.com",
    extra={
        "cpf": "123.456.789-00",
        "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxIn0.c2ln",
        "plan": "free",
    },
)
try:
    raise ValueError("user ana@example.com not found")
except ValueError:
    log.exception("login failed")

Output (captured by running the example, Python 3.11):

{"timestamp": "...", "level": "INFO", "logger": "app.signup", "message": "code sent to [REDACTED]", "cpf": "[REDACTED]", "access_token": "[REDACTED]", "plan": "free"}
{"timestamp": "...", "level": "ERROR", "logger": "app.signup", "message": "login failed", "exception": "Traceback (most recent call last):\n  File \"...\", line ..., in <module>\nValueError: user [REDACTED] not found"}

redact=True uses the default policy; RedactionPolicy(...) adds what belongs to your domain. What it does:

  • Sensitive keys — every extra= field, and every key of a dict passed as an argument or nested in a value, whose name contains a fragment of DEFAULT_REDACT_KEYS (password, token, secret, signature, authorization, cookie, email, api_key, ...) has its whole value replaced. Matching is by substring, lower-cased with - turned into _: access_token, X-API-Key and Set-Cookie all match.
  • Text patterns — the message, arguments, traceback (exc_text), stack_info and every string value go through e-mail, Bearer <credential>, JWT and the token segment of the routes the SDK itself mounts with a credential in the URL (/activate/<token>, /password-reset/<token>, /email-change/<token>, /email-verify/<token> — it reads /password-reset/[REDACTED]), plus key=value / key: value when the key is sensitive (?token=abc in a query, {'password': 'x'} quoted in an exception).
  • extra_keys / extra_patterns add without restating the defaults; keys / patterns replace them. String patterns are compiled at construction.
  • exact_keys compares by equality, for a short name a substring would over-match: with RedactionPolicy(exact_keys={"code"}), "GET /invite?code=123456 status_code=200" comes out as "GET /invite?code=[REDACTED] status_code=200" — code is hidden, the response status stays. It applies to extra= and nested dicts too.

The filter goes on every handler configure_logging installs — stdout and the six files — and not on the logger: a logger's filters do not run for records propagated from a child logger, a handler's do. A handler you attach yourself (Sentry, syslog) gets the same filter like this:

import logging
import sys

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import RedactionFilter, RedactionPolicy

handler: logging.Handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stderr)
handler.addFilter(RedactionFilter(RedactionPolicy(extra_keys={"cpf"})))
logging.getLogger().addHandler(handler)

What changes on the record

Redaction rewrites the LogRecord in place: msg becomes the rendered, redacted message and args is cleared. Anything that groups logs by template ("code sent to %s") sees the final message instead. And substring matching errs on the side of hiding: email_verified and token_type come out as [REDACTED] too.

Cost

Measured with configure_logging(file_output=False) writing to /dev/null, 20,000 records, best of 5 runs, Python 3.11: a line shaped like the AccessLogMiddleware one (message with 4 arguments, 7 extra= fields) went from ~13.5 µs to ~26 µs; a logger.exception with a short traceback, from ~44 µs to ~66 µs. A record is redacted once, not once per handler. With redact=False (the default) no filter is installed.

JSONFormatter changed for this to work: the exception field comes from record.exc_text when an earlier step already rendered it — the same precedence as the stdlib logging.Formatter — rather than from exc_info again. Before, a handler filter that redacted the traceback was overwritten with the original text. In LogSettings, LOG_REDACT=true turns the default policy on through logging_kwargs().

docs.title: exc_info on every level, and the name LogRecord will not give up
docs.text:
debug, info, warning, error and critical all take exc_info as a named parameter — a bool or "auto":

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils

logger: LogUtils = LogUtils(__name__)


def refresh_cache(key: str) -> None:
    """Reload one entry, tolerating an unavailable cache."""
    try:
        raise ConnectionError("redis down")
    except ConnectionError:
        logger.warning("Cache miss on %s", key, exc_info="auto", op="refresh")

Up to 0.280.0 that line was a dormant KeyError

Only error had the parameter. On the other four levels exc_info= fell into **fields, became extra=, and logging refuses to overwrite a reserved LogRecord attribute — inside makeRecord, after the level check. Measured on 0.280.0:

level ERROR, warning(exc_info=...) call: does NOT raise
level DEBUG, same call -> KeyError: "Attempt to overwrite 'exc_info'
                                     in LogRecord"

A service running at INFO carried the failure asleep until someone raised the verbosity — which is to say it went off during the incident, the minute the log was the only tool left.

This holds for any name LogRecord already uses, not just exc_info: stack_info, msg, args, levelname, name, asctime and more. A field by one of those names is now refused at the call, with TypeError, regardless of level:

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import LogUtils

logger: LogUtils = LogUtils(__name__)

try:
    logger.info("order processed", levelname="FAKE")
except TypeError as error:
    print(error)

LogUtils: reserved LogRecord attribute used as a structured field:
'levelname'. logging would raise KeyError while building the record — after
the level check, so the failure stays dormant until the verbosity goes up.
Rename the field, or pass exc_info= as the named parameter every level method
accepts.

The set of names is read off a real LogRecord rather than typed out, so it tracks the interpreter. Measured: 22 names on 3.11, 23 on 3.12 and 3.13 — the addition is taskName, which does not exist on 3.11.

Rename the field, not the intent

Need a structured field with that meaning? Prefix it: op_name instead of name, record_args instead of args. The name logging reserves belongs to the record's machinery, not to your domain.

docs.title: After Alembic — reinitialize_logging
docs.text:
logging.config.fileConfig() disables, by default, every logger that already existed. The env.py this SDK ships calls exactly that, so a migration run silences the application's own loggers for the rest of the process — records are dropped before any handler sees them, which looks like a logging configuration problem and is not one.

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import reinitialize_logging

reinitialize_logging()

Call it after any code that reconfigures Python's logging system. It re-enables the loggers and clears the "root already configured" latch, so the next LogUtils(...) installs handlers again.

docs.title: Reading logs over HTTP — make_logs_router
docs.text:
make_logs_router mounts GET /logs, which parses the on-disk JSON files and returns a paginated BasePaginationSchema[LogEntrySchema] (newest first).

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import make_logs_router

from src.core.settings import settings

app = FastAPI()


app.include_router(
    make_logs_router(log_dir="logs", token_secret=settings.TOKEN_SECRET),
)

An empty secret is refused

GET /logs exposes tracebacks and request metadata, and DELETE /logs truncates the files. Both require the X-Token header, compared against token_secret via make_token_dependency — or your own dependencies= (see "Behind your own auth" below). An empty (or whitespace-only) token_secret without dependencies= makes make_logs_router raise ValueError at construction: the app fails to start instead of starting with /logs open. Fill TOKEN_SECRET with uv run tempest secrets init.

The service generated by tempest new mounts /logs only when TOKEN_SECRET is not empty, because its .env.example ships TOKEN_SECRET= blank.

For a local run nothing else can reach, the refusal is turned off by name, where the reader of the call sees it:

from fastapi import FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import make_logs_router

app = FastAPI()


app.include_router(
    make_logs_router(log_dir="logs", allow_unauthenticated=True),
)

With token_secret set, allow_unauthenticated has no effect: a request without X-Token still gets 401.

Query examples:

# Latest 20 records across every level
curl -H "X-Token: $TOKEN_SECRET" "http://localhost:8000/logs"

# Only the isolated 500s, page 1, 50 per page
curl -H "X-Token: $TOKEN_SECRET" "http://localhost:8000/logs?source=500&page_size=50"

# Errors mentioning "timeout" in a time window
curl -H "X-Token: $TOKEN_SECRET" \
  "http://localhost:8000/logs?source=error&q=timeout&start=2026-05-31T00:00:00Z"

Query parameters:

Parameter Values Description source all (default), debug, info, warning, error, critical, 500 Which file to read. all merges every level; 500 returns only the isolated 500s. q text Case-insensitive substring match on the message. start / end ISO-8601 Limit records to a time window. A value with no offset (2026-05-31T00:00:00, or a bare date) is read as UTC. page / page_size integers Pagination (1-indexed).

The read is bounded per file

Each request reads the newest 20,000 records of every selected level (DEFAULT_MAX_RECORDS_PER_FILE) — the current file and its rotated backups together, newest first — not the whole history. The endpoint sorts newest-first and paginates, so what was left out was unreachable anyway — and without the bound a multi-gigabyte log directory went into memory whole on every request, taking the worker down before it answered. Tune it with make_logs_router(max_records_per_file=...); when the cap bites, a WARNING is logged naming the source.

docs.title: Clearing — DELETE /logs
docs.text:
The same router mounts the opposite verb, behind the same X-Token:

# Empty one level
curl -X DELETE -H "X-Token: $TOKEN_SECRET" \
  "http://localhost:8000/logs?source=info"

# Empty everything, 500.log included
curl -X DELETE -H "X-Token: $TOKEN_SECRET" \
  "http://localhost:8000/logs"

The response names what it emptied:

{"cleared": ["debug.log", "info.log", "warning.log", "error.log", "critical.log", "500.log"]}

all reaches 500.log here; on the read, it does not

It is the one place the two verbs disagree, and it is deliberate. Reading all does not include 500.log because every record in it is also in error.log — the page would list the same record twice. Clearing all does include it, because a clear that left the 500 stream behind is the surprising outcome.

Truncates, never unlinks — except the backups, if you ask

The handlers configure_logging installed hold an open descriptor on each path. Removing the file would leave them writing to an inode nothing can read back — the endpoint would look like it worked exactly once. A missing file is created empty, so the post-condition is the same.

Rotated backups (info.log.1, info.log.2026-10-20) are left intact by default: deleted history does not come back. Since the read includes them, the page keeps showing the earlier periods after a clear. To delete them too, ask explicitly — DELETE /logs?delete_backups=true or clear_log_files(..., delete_backups=True) — and they are listed in cleared right after their level's file.

An empty log_dir never becomes the current directory

LOG_DIR="" turns file logging off, but Path("") is .. So make_logs_router(log_dir="") and clear_log_files("") raise ValueError, the read (read_log_entries("")) returns nothing, and the /admin/logs page shows the empty state — none of them reads or truncates the *.log of wherever the process was started.

Anything that needs the paths outside a route — an archiving job, a collector, a counter — uses the same resolver the router uses, instead of re-deriving the level-to-filename map:

from pathlib import Path

from tempest_fastapi_sdk.api.routers.logs import resolve_log_files

paths: list[Path] = resolve_log_files("logs", "error")
every: list[Path] = resolve_log_files("logs", "all", include_http_500=True)

docs.title: Behind your own auth — dependencies=
docs.text:
A service that already has its own login (an admin Bearer JWT, a role, a session) does not need to invent a shared secret just for the logs. Pass the dependency that already guards the rest of the panel in dependencies=, and it applies to GET and DELETE:

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    JWTUtils,
    configure_logging,
    make_logs_router,
    make_role_dependency,
    register_exception_handlers,
)

configure_logging(log_dir="logs")

tokens: JWTUtils = JWTUtils(secret="a-32-character-secret-for-tests!")
require_admin = make_role_dependency(tokens, ["admin"])

app: FastAPI = FastAPI()
register_exception_handlers(app)
app.include_router(
    make_logs_router(log_dir="logs", dependencies=[Depends(require_admin)]),
)

What each call gets, measured against that app:

Request Response no Authorization 401 (UNAUTHORIZED) Bearer with roles: ["user"] 403 (FORBIDDEN) Bearer with roles: ["admin"] 200, no X-Token at all

Each item takes either spelling, Depends(require_admin) or just require_admin. A ready Depends is used as given, not wrapped again.

How dependencies= lives with X-Token

The two pieces add up; neither cancels the other:

  • Only dependencies=: they are the whole gate. No X-Token is read, and the header does not even show up in the OpenAPI schema.
  • token_secret and dependencies=: the request needs the header and has to pass every dependency.
  • Neither: ValueError at construction, as before, unless you pass allow_unauthenticated=True. An empty list (dependencies=[]) does not count as a gate.

docs.title: Another response contract — read_log_entries and clear_log_files
docs.text:
The router is a shell over two public functions. When the panel needs another response shape, call them directly instead of rewriting the read: the per-file cap lives there, and a hand-written reader that loads each file whole works on a fresh directory and kills the worker on a multi-gigabyte one.

Both are synchronous (file I/O). In an async route, run them off the event loop with asyncio.to_thread:

import asyncio

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import (
    JWTUtils,
    LogReadResult,
    clear_log_files,
    make_role_dependency,
    read_log_entries,
)

tokens: JWTUtils = JWTUtils(secret="a-32-character-secret-for-tests!")
require_admin = make_role_dependency(tokens, ["admin"])


class AppLogsResponseSchema(BaseModel):
    messages: list[str]
    truncated: bool


router: APIRouter = APIRouter(
    prefix="/api/admin/metrics",
    dependencies=[Depends(require_admin)],
)


@router.get("/app-logs")
async def app_logs(q: str | None = None, limit: int = 100) -> AppLogsResponseSchema:
    result: LogReadResult = await asyncio.to_thread(
        read_log_entries, "logs", "error", q=q
    )
    return AppLogsResponseSchema(
        messages=[str(entry["message"]) for entry in result.entries[:limit]],
        truncated=result.truncated,
    )


@router.delete("/app-logs")
async def clear_app_logs() -> list[str]:
    return await asyncio.to_thread(clear_log_files, "logs", "error")


app: FastAPI = FastAPI()
app.include_router(router)

With a logger.error("payment gateway timeout") on disk, an admin's GET /api/admin/metrics/app-logs?q=timeout answered:

{"messages": ["payment gateway timeout"], "truncated": false}

and the DELETE answered ["error.log"].

  • read_log_entries(log_dir, source="all", *, q, start, end, max_records_per_file) returns a LogReadResult: entries, already filtered and newest first, and truncated, which says whether the cap cut any file. Nothing matched? entries is [].
  • clear_log_files(log_dir, source="all") truncates in place and returns the names it emptied. For "all", 500.log is included — the same rule as DELETE /logs.

Recap

  • configure_logging(log_dir=...) → stdout + one file per level.
  • Exact-level routing: each file holds only its own severity.
  • 500.log isolates uncaught 500s (the http_500 marker).
  • make_logs_router serves those files, paginated and authenticated — by X-Token or by your own auth in dependencies=.
  • read_log_entries / clear_log_files are the read and the clear without the router, for another response contract.

docs.title: One line per request — AccessLogMiddleware
docs.text:
configure_logging formats what you log and RequestIDMiddleware binds the correlation id, but none of that emits the one line per request that makes make_logs_router worth reading. That is what AccessLogMiddleware is for:

# src/api/app.py
import logging

from fastapi import FastAPI
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AccessLogMiddleware, RequestIDMiddleware

app: FastAPI = FastAPI()

app.add_middleware(AccessLogMiddleware, level=logging.INFO)
app.add_middleware(RequestIDMiddleware)

Every request becomes a record whose message is the familiar line (GET /api/users 200 12.4ms) and whose details go through extra= as real fields — http_method, http_path, http_query, http_status, duration_ms, client_ip. That difference is what makes JSONFormatter write keys rather than an interpolated string, and therefore what lets GET /logs filter on them.

Registration order no longer matters (since v0.277.0)

The request_id comes from two sources, because neither alone survives both orders: the context variable RequestIDMiddleware binds, and the header it stamps on the response. Measured:

AccessLogMiddleware inside RequestIDMiddleware   context variable: set
                                                 response header:  not yet written
AccessLogMiddleware outside RequestIDMiddleware  context variable: cleared
                                                 response header:  present

RequestIDMiddleware is a BaseHTTPMiddleware: it stamps the header after the app returns, so an inner middleware's send wrapper has already run; and it clears the context variable as it unwinds, so an outer one finds nothing there. Reading both covers both.

Up to v0.276.0 this was a !!! danger telling you to register in the right order. A warning about a mechanical step with one right answer is code that was not written — the repository's own rule caught the SDK itself.

docs.title: Level: ERROR is where the failure is
docs.text:
A response below 500 is logged at the level you configured (INFO by default). A 5xx is logged at ERROR — both the one the application rendered and the one that escaped a handler. Finding failed requests by filtering on level is the reason to write these lines at all.

The escaping exception is the case that most needs a log line and the one hand-written versions most often miss: the handler blew up before sending anything, so there is no status to read. The middleware records 500, adds an error field naming the exception class, and re-raises — your own error handling still decides what the client sees.

docs.title: A stream is not a one-hour request
docs.text:
# src/api/app.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AccessLogMiddleware

app: FastAPI = FastAPI()

app.add_middleware(
    AccessLogMiddleware,
    exempt_paths=("/api/sse", "/api/metrics"),
)

exempt_paths matches by prefix, so ("/api/sse",) covers /api/sse/stream. An SSE connection held open for an hour would otherwise be logged, on close, as a request that took an hour.

docs.title: A secret in the URL is already logged
docs.text:
A deprecated endpoint that took a bearer-equivalent token as a path parameter reaches the middleware with the token in the URL — refusing the request in the handler does not un-log it.

The credential-bearing URLs the SDK itself issues are hidden by default, with no configuration: the token segment of /activate/{token}, /password-reset/{token}, /email-change/{token} and /email-verify/{token} (the e-mailed link under AUTH_BACKEND_LINKS=True only checks the token without consuming it, so it stays redeemable after the visit) and the value of every signature= or *token= query parameter, such as a signed URL's signature. The line reads GET /auth/password-reset/[REDACTED] 200. This is redact_capability_url, switched on by redact_capability_urls=True (the default); turn it off only if everyone who reads the log may also redeem those links.

For a secret of your own in the URL, redact is the seam, applied to the path and the query separately, after the redaction above:

# src/api/app.py
import re

from fastapi import FastAPI
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AccessLogMiddleware

_LEGACY_TOKEN_PATH: re.Pattern[str] = re.compile(
    r"^(?P<prefix>/api)?/auth/google/[^/]+$"
)

app: FastAPI = FastAPI()


def redact_path(value: str) -> str:
    """Replace the secret segment of a legacy path before it is logged."""
    if _LEGACY_TOKEN_PATH.match(value):
        return _LEGACY_TOKEN_PATH.sub(r"\g<prefix>/auth/google/<redacted>", value)
    return value


app.add_middleware(AccessLogMiddleware, redact=redact_path)

docs.title: Behind a proxy
docs.text:
# src/api/app.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from tempest_fastapi_sdk import AccessLogMiddleware

app: FastAPI = FastAPI()

app.add_middleware(AccessLogMiddleware, trusted_ip_header="x-real-ip")

client_ip comes from get_client_ip_from_scope. Never point trusted_ip_header at a bare X-Forwarded-For: that header is appended to whatever the client sent, so its leftmost entry is attacker-chosen — and the log would start attributing requests to whatever address they picked. See Security ».

Recap

  • AccessLogMiddleware is pure ASGI: it reads the status off http.response.start and leaves the exception path untouched.
  • The request_id reaches the line in either registration order: from the context variable when inner, from the response header when outer.
  • 5xx (rendered or escaped) is logged at ERROR; everything else at the configured level.
  • exempt_paths matches by prefix — that is what keeps SSE out of the log.
  • The SDK's capability-route tokens and signature= / *token= query values come out as [REDACTED] by default; redact rewrites the rest of path and query before the record exists.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• configure_logging writes structured JSON to stdout and to logs/, one file per level, each file carrying only its own level.
  • 500.log is isolated on purpose: the file you open first during an incident does not arrive mixed with everything else.
  • The request id lands on every line, so a user complaint becomes a grep — that is what separates structured logging from pretty logging.
  • make_logs_router mounts a paginated GET /logs over those files, newest first, so you can read them without shell access to the container.
  • A 5xx traceback does not carry the database's text: redact_database_errors swaps the DETAIL line that quotes the value for constraint and columns, and on_server_error still receives the original exception.
  • Every level takes exc_info (bool or "auto"); a structured field that collides with a LogRecord attribute is refused at the call, with TypeError.
  • With redact=True (or a RedactionPolicy), every handler redacts e-mails, Bearer, JWTs, the SDK's capability-route tokens and sensitive keys from the message, extra=, traceback and stack_info before the record is written.

docs.title: Management commands (project tempest <cmd>)
docs.text: Plug your own commands into the tempest CLI — the way Django lets you register manage.py <command>. A backfill script, a custom seed, a "reprocess the queue": each becomes tempest backfill, with the same help and error handling as the built-in commands.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Every service accumulates loose operational scripts (scripts/backfill.py, python -m app.tools.resync). Each with its own way to run, no --help, no convention. There was no canonical home: the same CLI that already runs tempest db upgrade and tempest check-config.

docs.title: Convention: src/commands.py
docs.text:
Expose a typer.Typer named commands in a src/commands.py module (or app/commands.py, or commands.py at the root):

import typer

commands: typer.Typer = typer.Typer()


@commands.command("backfill")
def backfill(dry_run: bool = False) -> None:
    """Recompute the denormalized counters."""
    typer.echo(f"backfill (dry_run={dry_run})")

Run it from the project root:

tempest backfill --dry-run

It shows up in tempest --help alongside the built-ins. The full power of Typer is available: arguments, options, types, help — all typed.

docs.title: Pointing at the location
docs.text:
Auto-detects src.commands / app.commands / commands. For another location (or several), configure it in pyproject.toml:

[tool.tempest]
commands = "src.management"
# or several modules:
commands = ["src.billing.commands", "src.ops.commands"]

docs.title: Collision with a built-in command
docs.text: If a project command has the same name as a built-in (new, db, check, check-config, version, …), the built-in wins and the project one is skipped with a warning on stderr. Pick another name.

docs.title: Nested groups
docs.text:
Since it is plain Typer, you can group. A sub-Typer becomes tempest ops <cmd>:

import typer

commands: typer.Typer = typer.Typer()
ops: typer.Typer = typer.Typer()
commands.add_typer(ops, name="ops")


@ops.command("resync")
def resync() -> None:
    """Reprocess the sync queue."""
    ...

tempest ops resync

Discovery is best-effort, but errors surface

With no command module, the CLI runs as usual. If you configured [tool.tempest] commands and the module fails to import (or exposes no Typer), tempest warns on stderr — but never stops running the built-in commands because of it.

Run from the project root

Discovery adds the current directory to sys.path to import src.commands. Run tempest from the project root (where pyproject.toml lives), as you already do for tempest db / check-config.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Expose commands: typer.Typer in src/commands.py; it becomes tempest <cmd>.
  • [tool.tempest] commands points at another module (string or list).
  • Collision with a built-in → built-in wins, project one skipped with a warning.
  • Plain Typer: args/options/types/help/nested groups for free.

docs.title: Mercado Pago: test accounts and credentials
docs.text:
Before charging for real, you want to see a Pix being created, a card being approved and another declined, a refund going back. All of that can be done in Mercado Pago's sandbox without moving money. The hard part is getting there: the dashboard has several credentials with similar names, and most combinations do not work for charging.

This page is the path that worked, step by step, with the error each detour produces. At the end you will have two things:

  1. a test seller account (who receives);
  2. its Access Token, from an application of the right type.

That is all. The payer can be any valid e-mail — measured, in step 5.

Measured, not deduced

Every answer quoted here was observed against the sandbox between 2026-10-09 and 2026-10-10, on the Orders API, with the credential and body described. The record is in vendor/mercadopago-evidence.md, section 9. Mercado Pago's dashboard changes from time to time: if a menu is not where this page says, search for the option's name.

docs.title: Why not use your own account
docs.text:
The first temptation is the TEST-... token shown under "Test credentials" of your application. It reads data, but it does not charge:

Credential Payer What the Orders API answers TEST- from your account anyone, or none 403 At least one policy returned UNAUTHORIZED. test seller's APP_USR-, Checkout Pro application any 401 Unauthorized use of live credentials (measured on the Payments API) test seller's APP_USR-, Checkout Transparente / Orders API application any valid e-mail 201, charge created

Only the last row charges. The rest of this page is how to get there.

Never use your real account's production credentials

The APP_USR-... of your account moves real money. Everything here uses the APP_USR-... of a test account, which has the same prefix but moves nothing. How to check is in step 6.

docs.title: Step 1 — create the test seller account
docs.text:
Log in with your normal account at https://www.mercadopago.com.br/developers/panel/test-users and create an account of type Seller, country Brazil. Write down what the dashboard shows: username, password and User ID.

What about the buyer account?

Charging through the API does not need one: the order's payer can be any valid e-mail (step 5). Create one only to test a screen where someone logs into Mercado Pago to pay.

docs.title: Step 2 — log in as the seller
docs.text:
Open a private window (so it does not mix with your real account) and log in at https://www.mercadopago.com.br/ with the seller's username and password.

If Mercado Pago asks for a verification code, use the last 6 digits of the test account's User ID.

docs.title: Step 3 — create an application of the right type
docs.text:
Still logged in as the seller, open https://www.mercadopago.com.br/developers/panel/app and click Create application:

  1. Solution: choose Checkout Transparente. Do not choose Checkout Pro: its token creates checkout preferences but refuses direct charges with 401 Unauthorized use of live credentials.
  2. API type: choose Orders API. The Payments API shows the warning "This API will be discontinued soon", and this SDK talks to Orders.
  3. Name: anything.

docs.title: Step 4 — copy the seller's Access Token
docs.text:
In the new application, open Production credentials and copy the Access Token (APP_USR-...).

It is the production token of a test account, and it is exactly the one you want. Two paths that look right and are not:

  • "Test credentials" inside the test account: the dashboard answers "Não é possível utilizar credenciais de teste em um ambiente de teste" (test credentials cannot be used in a test environment).
  • "Activate credentials": in a test account the option does not show, and it is not needed.

Keep the token outside any repository, readable only by you:

mkdir -p ~/.config/my-service
printf 'MERCADO_PAGO_TEST_SELLER_ACCESS_TOKEN=APP_USR-paste-here\n' \
  > ~/.config/my-service/mercadopago-sandbox.env
chmod 600 ~/.config/my-service/mercadopago-sandbox.env

Open the file in your editor and replace the value. Never paste the token into a chat, a commit or a log.

docs.title: Step 5 — the payer's e-mail
docs.text:
With the right token, an order accepts any valid e-mail as the payer: buyer@example.com, a Gmail, a made-up test_user_…@testuser.com — Pix and card, all 201. What it refuses is not having one:

payer sent Answer absent, or {} 400 '$.payer' - minimum 1 properties allowed, but found 0 properties only first_name 400 '$.payer.email' or '$.payer.customer_id' or '$.payer.id' the TESTUSER… username instead of an e-mail 400 '$.payer.email' - does not match pattern any valid e-mail 201

If you saw other payer errors

500 payer_cannot_be_nil, 400 excludes_by_rule and 403 Payer email forbidden were measured on the Payments API (/v1/payments), which requires an actual test buyer. If they show up, the code is calling the discontinued API.

docs.title: Step 6 — check it worked
docs.text:
The script below does two things. First, it checks the token belongs to a test account — if not, it stops without charging anything. Then it creates a R$ 19.90 Pix through the Orders API and cancels it right away.

import asyncio
import os
import uuid
from typing import Any

from tempest_fastapi_sdk import HTTPClient

BASE_URL: str = "https://api.mercadopago.com"


async def main() -> None:
    """Check the token is a test account, then open and cancel a Pix order."""
    token: str = os.environ["MERCADO_PAGO_TEST_SELLER_ACCESS_TOKEN"]
    async with HTTPClient(
        base_url=BASE_URL,
        default_headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"},
    ) as http:
        me: dict[str, Any] = (await http.request("GET", "/users/me")).json()
        if "test_user" not in (me.get("tags") or []):
            raise SystemExit("This token is not a test account. Stopping.")

        created = await http.request(
            "POST",
            "/v1/orders",
            headers={"X-Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4())},
            json={
                "type": "online",
                "processing_mode": "automatic",
                "total_amount": "19.90",
                "external_reference": "sandbox-check-1",
